A New Way To Pay Old Debts

Philip Massinger — EMOTHE0309_ANewWayToPayOldDebts

Dramatis Personae

  • Lovell, an English lord
  • Sir Giles Overreach, a cruel extortioner
  • [Frank] Wellborn, a prodigal [nephew to Overreach]
  • [Tom] Allworth, a young gentleman, page to Lord Lovell [and stepson to Lady Allworth]
  • Greedy, a hungry justice of peace
  • [Jack] Marall, a term driver, a creature of Sir Giles Overreach
  • Order, [a steward] }
  • Amble, [an usher] } servants to the Lady Allworth
  • Furnace, [a cook] }
  • Watchall, [a porter] }
  • Willdo, a parson
  • Tapwell, an alehouse-keeper
  • Three Creditors
  • The Lady Allworth, a rich widow [Tom Allworth’s stepmother]
  • Margaret, Overreach his daughter
  • Waiting-woman, } [to Lady Allworth]
  • Chambermaid, }
  • Froth, Tapwell’s wife
  • [Servants]

[THE SCENE: The countryside near Nottingham]

1.1

[Enter] Wellborn [in ragged clothes], Tapwell, [and] Froth.

WELLBORN

1No booze? Nor no tobacco?

TAPWELL

No booze? Nor no tobacco? Not a suck, sir,
2Nor the remainder of a single can
3Left by a drunken porter, all night palled too.

FROTH

4Not the dropping of the tap for your morning's draft, sir.
5'Tis verity, I assure you.

WELLBORN

'Tis verity, I assure you. Verity, you brach!
6The devil turned precisian? Rogue, what am I?

TAPWELL

7Troth, durst I trust you with a looking glass
8To let you see your trim shape, you would quit me
9And take the name yourself.

WELLBORN

And take the name yourself. How, dog?

TAPWELL

And take the name yourself. How, dog? Even so, sir.
10And I must tell you, if you but advance
11Your Plymouth cloak, you shall be soon instructed
12There dwells—and within call, if it please Your Worship—
13A potent monarch called the constable,
14That does command a citadel called the stocks,
15Whose guards are certain files of rusty billmen,
16Such as with great dexterity will hale
17Your tattered, lousy—

WELLBORN

Your tattered, lousy— Rascal! Slave!

FROTH

Your tattered, lousy— Rascal! Slave! No rage, sir.

TAPWELL

18[to Froth] At his own peril. [To Wellborn] Do not put yourself
19In too much heat, there being no water near
20To quench your thirst; and sure, for other liquor,
21As mighty ale or beer, they are things, I take it,
22You must no more remember—not in a dream, sir.

WELLBORN

23Why, thou unthankful villain, dar'st thou talk thus?
24Is not thy house, and all thou hast, my gift?

TAPWELL

25I find it not in chalk, and Timothy Tapwell
26Does keep no other register.

WELLBORN

Does keep no other register. Am not I he
27Whose riots fed and clothed thee? Wert thou not
28Born on my father's land, and proud to be
29A drudge in his house?

TAPWELL

A drudge in his house? What I was, sir, it skills not.
30What you are is apparent. Now for a farewell:
31Since you talk of father, in my hope it will torment you,
32I'll briefly tell your story. Your dead father,
33My quondam master, was a man of worship,
34Old Sir John Wellborn, Justice of Peace and Quorum,
35And stood fair to be Custos Rotulorum,
36Bare the whole sway of the shire, kept a great house,
37Relieved the poor, and so forth; but he dying,
38And the twelve hundred a year coming to you,
39Late Master Francis, but now forlorn Wellborn—

WELLBORN

40Slave, stop, or I shall lose myself.

FROTH

Slave, stop, or I shall lose myself. Very hardly;
41You cannot out of your way.

TAPWELL

You cannot out of your way. But to my story.
42You were then a lord of acres, the prime gallant,
43And I your under-butler. Note the change now.
44You had a merry time of't—hawks and hounds,
45With choice of running horses, mistresses
46Of all sort and all sizes—yet so hot
47As their embraces made your lordship melt.
48Which your uncle, Sir Giles Overreach, observing,
49Resolving not to lose a drop of 'em
50On foolish mortgages, statutes, and bonds,
51For a while supplied your looseness, and then left you.

WELLBORN

52Some curate hath penned this invective, mongrel,
53And you have studied it.

TAPWELL

And you have studied it. I have not done yet.
54Your land gone, and your credit not worth a token,
55You grew the common borrower; no man scaped
56Your paper pellets, from the gentleman
57To the beggars on highways, that sold you switches
58In your gallantry.

WELLBORN

In your gallantry. I shall switch your brains out.

TAPWELL

59Where poor Tim Tapwell, with a little stock,
60Some forty pounds or so, bought a small cottage,
61Humbled myself to marriage with my Froth here,
62Gave entertainment—

WELLBORN

Gave entertainment— Yes, to whores and canters,
63Clubbers by night.

TAPWELL

Clubbers by night. True, but they brought in profit,
64And had a gift to pay for what they called for,
65And stuck not like Your Mastership. The poor income
66I gleaned from them hath made me in my parish
67Thought worthy to be scavenger, and in time
68May rise to be overseer of the poor—
69Which if I do, on your petition, Wellborn,
70I may allow you thirteenpence a quarter,
71And you shall thank My Worship.

WELLBORN

And you shall thank My Worship. Thus, you dogbolt!
72And thus!

Beats and kicks him.

TAPWELL

And thus! [to Froth] Cry out for help!

WELLBORN

And thus! [to Froth] Cry out for help! Stir, and thou diest.
73Your potent prince, the constable, shall not save you.
74Hear me, ungrateful hellhound. Did not I
75Make purses for you? Then you licked my boots,
76And thought your holiday cloak too coarse to clean 'em.
77'Twas I that, when I heard thee swear if ever
78Thou couldst arrive at forty pounds thou wouldst
79Live like an emperor, 'twas I that gave it
80In ready gold. Deny this, wretch!

TAPWELL

In ready gold. Deny this, wretch! I must sir,
81For, from the tavern to the taphouse, all,
82On forfeiture of their licenses, stand bound
83Never to remember who their best guests were,
84If they grew poor like you.

WELLBORN

If they grew poor like you. They are well rewarded
85That beggar themselves to make such cuckolds rich.
86Thou viper, thankless viper! Impudent bawd!
87But since you are grown forgetful, I will help
88Your memory, and tread thee into mortar,
89Not leave one bone unbroken.

[He beats Tapwell again.]

TAPWELL

Not leave one bone unbroken. Oh!

FROTH

Not leave one bone unbroken. Oh! Ask mercy!

Enter Allworth.

WELLBORN

90'Twill not be granted.

ALLWORTH

'Twill not be granted. Hold, for my sake, hold!
91Deny me, Frank? They are not worth your anger.

WELLBORN

92For once thou hast redeemed them from this scepter.

[Wellborn puts up] his cudgel.

93But let 'em vanish, creeping on their knees,
94And, if they grumble, I revoke my pardon.

FROTH

95This comes of your prating, husband. You presumed
96On your ambling wit, and must use your glib tongue
97Though you are beaten lame for't.

TAPWELL

Though you are beaten lame for't. Patience, Froth.
98There's law to cure our bruises.

They go off on their hands and knees.

WELLBORN

There's law to cure our bruises. Sent to your mother?

ALLWORTH

99My lady, Frank, my patroness! My all!
100She's such a mourner for my father's death,
101And, in her love to him, so favors me
102That I cannot pay too much observance to her.
103There are few such stepdames.

WELLBORN

There are few such stepdames. 'Tis a noble widow,
104And keeps her reputation pure and clear
105From the least taint of infamy; her life,
106With the splendor of her actions, leaves no tongue
107To envy or detraction. Prithee tell me:
108Has she no suitors?

ALLWORTH

Has she no suitors? Even the best of the shire, Frank,
109My lord excepted—such as sue and send,
110And send and sue again, but to no purpose.
111Their frequent visits have not gained her presence.
112Yet she's so far from sullenness and pride
113That I dare undertake you shall meet from her
114A liberal entertainment. I can give you
115A catalog of her suitors' names.

WELLBORN

A catalog of her suitors' names. Forbear it,
116While I give you good counsel. I am bound to it;
117Thy father was my friend, and that affection
118I bore to him, in right descends to thee.
119Thou art a handsome and a hopeful youth,
120Nor will I have the least affront stick on thee,
121If I with any danger can prevent it.

ALLWORTH

122I thank your noble care. But pray you, in what
123Do I run the hazard?

WELLBORN

Do I run the hazard? Art thou not in love?
124Put it not off with wonder.

ALLWORTH

Put it not off with wonder. In love, at my years?

WELLBORN

125You think you walk in clouds, but are transparent.
126I have heard all, and the choice that you have made,
127And with my finger can point out the north star
128By which the lodestone of your folly's guided.
129And to confirm this true, what think you of
130Fair Margaret, the only child and heir
131Of cormorant Overreach? Does it blush and start
132To hear her only named? Blush at your want
133Of wit and reason.

ALLWORTH

Of wit and reason. You are too bitter, sir.

WELLBORN

134Wounds of this nature are not to be cured
135With balms, but corrosives. I must be plain:
136Art thou scarce manumized from the porter's lodge,
137And yet sworn servant to the pantofle,
138And dar'st thou dream of marriage? I fear
139'Twill be concluded for impossible
140That there is now, nor e'er shall be hereafter,
141A handsome page or players' boy of fourteen
142But either loves a wench, or drabs love him—
143Court-waiters not exempted.

ALLWORTH

Court-waiters not exempted. This is madness.
144Howe'er you have discovered my intents,
145You know my aims are lawful; and if ever
146The queen of flowers, the glory of the spring,
147The sweetest comfort to our smell, the rose,
148Sprang from an envious brier, I may infer
149There's such disparity in their conditions
150Between the goddess of my soul, the daughter,
151And the base churl, her father.

WELLBORN

And the base churl, her father. Grant this true,
152As I believe it, canst thou ever hope
153To enjoy a quiet bed with her whose father
154Ruined thy state?

ALLWORTH

Ruined thy state? And yours too.

WELLBORN

Ruined thy state? And yours too. I confess it.
155True, I must tell you as a friend, and freely,
156That, where impossibilities are apparent,
157'Tis indiscretion to nourish hopes.
158Canst thou imagine—let not self-love blind thee—
159That Sir Giles Overreach, that, to make her great
160In swelling titles, without touch of conscience
161Will cut his neighbor's throat, and I hope his own too,
162Will e'er consent to make her thine? Give o'er,
163And think of some course suitable to thy rank,
164And prosper in it.

ALLWORTH

And prosper in it. You have well advised me.
165But in the meantime, you that are so studious
166Of my affairs wholly neglect your own.
167Remember yourself, and in what plight you are.

WELLBORN

168No matter, no matter.

ALLWORTH

No matter, no matter. Yes, 'tis much material.
169You know my fortune and my means; yet something
170I can spare from myself to help your wants.

[He offers money.]

WELLBORN

171How's this?

ALLWORTH

How's this? Nay, be not angry. There's eight pieces
172To put you in better fashion.

WELLBORN

To put you in better fashion. Money from thee?
173From a boy? A stipendiary? One that lives
174At the devotion of a stepmother
175And the uncertain favor of a lord?
176I'll eat my arms first. Howsoe'er blind Fortune
177Hath spent the utmost of her malice on me—
178Though I am vomited out of an alehouse,
179And, thus accoutred, know not where to eat,
180Or drink, or sleep, but underneath this canopy—
181Although I thank thee, I despise thy offer.
182And, as I in my madness broke my state
183Without th'assistance of another's brain,
184In my right wits I'll piece it; at the worst
185Die thus, and be forgotten.

ALLWORTH

Die thus, and be forgotten. A strange humor!

Exeunt.

1.2

[Enter] Order, Amble, Furnace, [and] Watchall.

ORDER

1Set all things right, or—as my name is Order,
2And by this staff of office that commands you,
3This chain and double ruff, symbols of power—
4Whoever misses in his function,
5For one whole week makes forfeiture of his breakfast
6And privilege in the wine cellar.

AMBLE

And privilege in the wine cellar. You are merry,
7Good Master Steward.

FURNACE

Good Master Steward. Let him; I'll be angry.

AMBLE

8Why, fellow Furnace, 'tis not twelve o'clock yet,
9Nor dinner taking up; then 'tis allowed
10Cooks by their places may be choleric.

FURNACE

11You think you have spoke wisely, goodman Amble,
12My lady's go-before!

ORDER

My lady's go-before! Nay, nay, no wrangling.

FURNACE

13Twit me with the authority of the kitchen?
14At all hours and all places I'll be angry;
15And, thus provoked, when I am at my prayers,
16I will be angry.

AMBLE

I will be angry. There was no hurt meant.

FURNACE

17I am friends with thee, and yet I will be angry.

ORDER

18With whom?

FURNACE

With whom? No matter whom. Yet, now I think on't,
19I am angry with my lady.

WATCHALL

I am angry with my lady. Heaven forbid, man!

ORDER

20What cause has she given thee?

FURNACE

What cause has she given thee? Cause enough, Master Steward.
21I was entertained by her to please her palate,
22And till she forswore eating I performed it.
23Now since our master, noble Allworth, died,
24Though I crack my brains to find out tempting sauces,
25And raise fortifications in the pastry
26Such as might serve for models in the Low Countries,
27Which if they had been practiced at Breda,
28Spinola might have thrown his cap at it and ne'er took it—

AMBLE

29But you had wanted matter there to work on.

FURNACE

30Matter? With six eggs and a strike of rye meal
31I had kept the town till doomsday, perhaps longer.

ORDER

32But, what's this to your pet against my lady?

FURNACE

33What's this? Marry, this: when I am three parts roasted
34And the fourth part parboiled to prepare her viands,
35She keeps her chamber, dines with a panada
36Or water-gruel, my sweat never thought on.

ORDER

37But your art is seen in the dining room.

FURNACE

But your art is seen in the dining room. By whom?
38By such as pretend love to her, but come
39To feed upon her. Yet of all the Harpies
40That do devour her, I am out of charity
41With none so much as the thin-gutted squire
42That's stol'n into commission.

ORDER

That's stol'n into commission. Justice Greedy?

FURNACE

43The same, the same. Meat's cast away upon him;
44It never thrives. He holds this paradox:
45Who eats not well can ne'er do justice well.
46His stomach's as insatiate as the grave,
47Or strumpet's ravenous appetites.

WATCHALL

Or strumpet's ravenous appetites. One knocks.

Allworth knocks, and enters.

ORDER

48Our late young master!

AMBLE

Our late young master! Welcome, sir.

FURNACE

Our late young master! Welcome, sir. Your hand.
49If you have a stomach, a cold bake-meat's ready.

ORDER

50[to the others] His father's picture in little.

FURNACE

[to the others] His father's picture in little. We are all your servants.

AMBLE

51In you he lives.

ALLWORTH

In you he lives. At once, my thanks to all.
52This is yet some comfort. Is my lady stirring?

ORDER

53Her presence answer for us.

Enter the Lady Allworth, Waiting-woman, [and] Chambermaid.

LADY ALLWORTH

Her presence answer for us. [to her women] Sort those silks well.
54I'll take the air alone.

Exeunt Waiting-woman and Chambermaid.

FURNACE

I'll take the air alone. You air and air,
55But will you never taste but spoon-meat more?
56To what use serve I?

LADY ALLWORTH

To what use serve I? Prithee, be not angry;
57I shall, ere long. I'the meantime, there is gold
58To buy thee aprons and a summer suit.

[She gives money.]

FURNACE

59I am appeased, and Furnace now grows cool.

LADY ALLWORTH

60And, as I gave directions, if this morning
61I am visited by any, entertain 'em
62As heretofore, but say, in my excuse,
63I am indisposed.

ORDER

I am indisposed. I shall, madam.

LADY ALLWORTH

I am indisposed. I shall, madam. Do, and leave me.—
64Nay, stay you, Allworth.

ALLWORTH

Nay, stay you, Allworth. I shall gladly grow here
65To wait on your commands.

Exeunt Order, Amble, Furnace, [and] Watchall.

LADY ALLWORTH

To wait on your commands. So soon turned courtier!

ALLWORTH

66Style not that "courtship", madam, which is duty
67Purchased on your part.

LADY ALLWORTH

Purchased on your part. Well, you shall o'ercome;
68I'll not contend in words. How is it with
69Your noble master?

ALLWORTH

Your noble master? Ever like himself,
70No scruple lessened in the full weight of honor.
71He did command me (pardon my presumption)
72As his unworthy deputy to kiss
73Your Ladyship's fair hands.

[He kisses her hands.]

LADY ALLWORTH

Your Ladyship's fair hands. I am honored in
74His favor to me. Does he hold his purpose
75For the Low Countries?

ALLWORTH

For the Low Countries? Constantly, good madam,
76But he will in person first present his service.

LADY ALLWORTH

77And how approve you of his course? You are yet,
78Like virgin parchment, capable of any
79Inscription, vicious or honorable.
80I will not force your will, but leave you free
81To your own election.

ALLWORTH

To your own election. Any form you please
82I will put on; but, might I make my choice,
83With humble emulation I would follow
84The path my lord marks to me.

LADY ALLWORTH

The path my lord marks to me. 'Tis well answered,
85And I commend your spirit. You had a father—
86Blessed be his memory!—that some few hours
87Before the will of heaven took him from me,
88Who did commend you, by the dearest ties
89Of perfect love between us, to my charge;
90And therefore what I speak you are bound to hear
91With such respect as if he lived in me.
92He was my husband, and howe'er you are not
93Son of my womb, you may be of my love,
94Provided you deserve it.

ALLWORTH

Provided you deserve it. I have found you,
95Most honored madam, the best mother to me,
96And, with my utmost strengths of care and service,
97Will labor that you never may repent
98Your bounties showered upon me.

LADY ALLWORTH

Your bounties showered upon me. I much hope it.
99These were your father's words: "If e'er my son
100Follow the war, tell him it is a school
101Where all the principles tending to honor
102Are taught, if truly followed; but for such
103As repair thither as a place in which
104They do presume they may with license practice
105Their lusts and riots, they shall never merit
106The noble name of soldiers. To dare boldly
107In a fair cause, and for the country's safety
108To run upon the cannon's mouth undaunted;
109To obey their leaders, and shun mutinies;
110To bear with patience the winter's cold
111And summer's scorching heat, and not to faint,
112When plenty of provision fails, with hunger,
113Are the essential parts make up a soldier—
114Not swearing, dice, or drinking."

ALLWORTH

Not swearing, dice, or drinking." There's no syllable
115You speak but is to me an oracle,
116Which but to doubt were impious.

LADY ALLWORTH

Which but to doubt were impious. To conclude:
117Beware ill company, for often men
118Are like to those with whom they do conserve.
119And from one man I warned you, and that's Wellborn;
120Not 'cause he's poor—that rather claims your pity—
121But that he's in his manners so debauched,
122And hath to vicious courses sold himself.
123'Tis true your father loved him while he was
124Worthy the loving, but, if he had lived
125To have seen him as he is, he had cast him off
126As you must do.

ALLWORTH

As you must do. I shall obey in all things.

LADY ALLWORTH

127Follow me to my chamber; you shall have gold
128To furnish you like my son, and still supplied
129As I hear from you.

ALLWORTH

As I hear from you. I am still your creature.

Exeunt.

1.3

[Enter] Overreach, Greedy, Order, Amble, Furnace, Watchall, [and] Marall.

GREEDY

1Not to be seen?

OVERREACH

Not to be seen? Still cloistered up? Her reason,
2I hope, assures her, though she make herself
3Close prisoner ever for her husband's loss,
4'Twill not recover him.

ORDER

'Twill not recover him. Sir, it is her will,
5Which we that are her servants ought to serve it
6And not dispute. Howe'er, you are nobly welcome,
7And, if you please to stay, that you may think so,
8There came not six days since from Hull a pipe
9Of rich canary, which shall spend itself
10For my lady's honor.

GREEDY

For my lady's honor. Is it of the right race?

ORDER

11Yes, Master Greedy.

AMBLE

Yes, Master Greedy. [aside to Furnace] How his mouth runs o'er!aparte

FURNACE

12[aside to Amble] I'll make it run, and run.—Save Your good Worship!aparte

GREEDY

13Honest Master Cook, thy hand again. How I love thee!
14Are the good dishes still in being? Speak, boy.

FURNACE

15If you have a mind to feed, there is a chine
16Of beef, well seasoned.

GREEDY

Of beef, well seasoned. Good!

FURNACE

Of beef, well seasoned. Good! A pheasant, larded.

GREEDY

17That I might now give thanks for't?

FURNACE

That I might now give thanks for't? Other kickshaws.
18Besides, there came last night from the Forest of Sherwood
19The fattest stag I ever cooked.

GREEDY

The fattest stag I ever cooked. A stag, man?

FURNACE

20A stag, sir—part of it prepared for dinner,
21And baked in puff paste.

GREEDY

And baked in puff paste. Puff paste too, Sir Giles!
22A ponderous chine of beef! A pheasant larded!
23And red deer too, Sir Giles, and baked in puff paste!
24All business set aside; let us give thanks here.

FURNACE

25[aside] How the lean skeleton's rapt!aparte

OVERREACH

[aside] How the lean skeleton's rapt! You know we cannot.

MARALL

26Your Worships are to sit on a commission,
27And, if you fail to come, you lose the cause.

GREEDY

28Cause me no causes. I'll prove't, for such a dinner
29We may put off a commission: you shall find it
30Henrici decimo quarto.

OVERREACH

Henrici decimo quarto. Fie, Master Greedy,
31Will you lose me a thousand pounds for a dinner?
32No more, for shame! We must forget the belly
33When we think of profit.

GREEDY

When we think of profit. Well, you shall o'errule me.
34I could ev'n cry now.—Do you hear, Master Cook?
35Send but a corner of that immortal pasty,
36And I, in thankfulness, will by your boy
37Send you a brace of threepences.

FURNACE

38[aside] Will you be so prodigal?aparte

Enter Wellborn.

OVERREACH

39Remember me to your lady.—Who have we here?

WELLBORN

40You know me.

OVERREACH

You know me. I did once, but now I will not;
41Thou art no blood of mine. Avaunt, thou beggar!
42If ever thou presume to own me more,
43I'll have thee caged and whipped.

GREEDY

I'll have thee caged and whipped. I'll grant the warrant.—
44Think of Pie Corner, Furnace!

Exeunt Overreach, Greedy, [and] Marall.

WATCHALL

Think of Pie Corner, Furnace! [to Wellborn] Will you out, sir?
45I wonder how you durst creep in.

ORDER

I wonder how you durst creep in. This is rudeness
46And saucy impudence.

AMBLE

And saucy impudence. Cannot you stay
47To be served among your fellows from the basket,
48But you must press into the hall?

FURNACE

But you must press into the hall? Prithee, vanish
49Into some outhouse, though it be the pigsty;
50My scullion shall come to thee.

Enter Allworth.

WELLBORN

My scullion shall come to thee. This is rare.
51Oh, here's Tom Allworth.—Tom!

ALLWORTH

Oh, here's Tom Allworth.—Tom! We must be strangers,
52Nor would I have you seen here for a million.

Exit Allworth.

WELLBORN

53Better and better. He contemns me too?

Enter [Waiting-] woman and Chambermaid.

WAITING-WOMAN

54Foh, what a smell's here! What thing's this?

CHAMBERMAID

Foh, what a smell's here! What thing's this? A creature
55Made out of the privy. Let us hence, for love's sake,
56Or I shall swoon.

WAITING-WOMAN

Or I shall swoon. I begin to faint already.

Exeunt [Waiting-] woman and Chambermaid.

WATCHALL

57[to Wellborn] Will you know your way?

AMBLE

[to Wellborn] Will you know your way? Or shall we teach it you
58By the head and shoulders?

WELLBORN

By the head and shoulders? No. I will not stir.
59Do you mark, I will not. Let me see the wretch
60That dares attempt to force me. Why, you slaves,
61Created only to make legs and cringe,
62To carry in a dish and shift a trencher,
63That have not souls only to hope a blessing
64Beyond blackjacks or flagons—you that were born
65Only to consume meat and drink, and batten
66Upon reversions! Who advances? Who
67Shows me the way?

ORDER

Shows me the way? My lady!

Enter Lady [Allworth, Waiting-] woman, [and] Chambermaid.

CHAMBERMAID

Shows me the way? My lady! Here's the monster.

WAITING-WOMAN

68Sweet madam, keep your glove to your nose.

CHAMBERMAID

Sweet madam, keep your glove to your nose. Or let me
69Fetch some perfumes may be predominant;
70You wrong yourself else.

WELLBORN

You wrong yourself else. Madam, my designs
71Bear me to you.

LADY ALLWORTH

Bear me to you. To me?

WELLBORN

Bear me to you. To me? And though I have met with
72But ragged entertainment from your grooms here,
73I hope from you to receive that noble usage
74As may become the true friend of your husband,
75And then I shall forget these.

LADY ALLWORTH

And then I shall forget these. I am amazed
76To see and hear this rudeness. Dar'st thou think,
77Though sworn, that it can ever find belief
78That I, who to the best men of this country
79Denied my presence since my husband's death,
80Can fall so low as to change words with thee?
81Thou son of infamy, forbear my house,
82And know and keep the distance that's between us,
83Or, though it be against my gentler temper,
84I shall take order you no more shall be
85An eyesore to me.

WELLBORN

An eyesore to me. Scorn me not, good lady;
86But, as in form you are angelical,
87Imitate the heavenly natures and vouchsafe
88At the least awhile to hear me. You will grant
89The blood that runs in this arm is as noble
90As that which fills your veins; those costly jewels,
91And those rich clothes you wear, your men's observance
92And women's flattery are in you no virtues,
93Nor these rags, with my poverty, in me vices.
94You have a fair fame, and, I know, deserve it—
95Yet, lady, I must say, in nothing more
96Than in the pious sorrow you have shown
97For your late noble husband.

ORDER

For your late noble husband. [aside to the others] How she starts!aparte

FURNACE

98[aside] And hardly can keep finger from eyeaparte
99To hear him named!

LADY ALLWORTH

To hear him named! Have you aught else to say?

WELLBORN

100That husband, madam, was once in his fortune
101Almost as low as I. Want, debts, and quarrels
102Lay heavy on him. Let it not be thought
103A boast in me though I say I relieved him.
104'Twas I that gave him fashion; mine the sword
105That did on all occasions second his;
106I brought him on and off with honor, lady.
107And when in all men's judgements he was sunk,
108And in his own hopes not to be buoyed up,
109I stepped unto him, took him by the hand,
110And set him upright.

FURNACE

And set him upright. [aside to the others] Are not we base rogues,aparte
111That could forget this?

WELLBORN

That could forget this? I confess you made him
112Master of your estate; nor could your friends,
113Though he brought no wealth with him, blame you for't,
114For he had a shape, and to that shape a mind
115Made up of all parts either great or noble—
116So winning a behavior not to be
117Resisted, madam.

LADY ALLWORTH

Resisted, madam. 'Tis most true. He had.

WELLBORN

118For his sake, then, in that I was his friend,
119Do not contemn me.

LADY ALLWORTH

Do not contemn me. For what's past, excuse me;
120I will redeem it.—Order, give the gentleman
121A hundred pounds.

WELLBORN

A hundred pounds. No, madam, on no terms.
122I will nor beg nor borrow sixpence of you,
123But be supplied elsewhere, or want thus ever.
124Only one suit I make, which you deny not
125To strangers; and 'tis this.

Whispers to her.

LADY ALLWORTH

To strangers; and 'tis this. Fie, nothing else?

WELLBORN

126Nothing, unless you please to charge your servants
127To throw away a little respect upon me.

LADY ALLWORTH

128What you demand is yours.

WELLBORN

What you demand is yours. I thank you, lady.
129Now what can be wrought out of such a suit
130Is yet in supposition. I have said all;
131When you please, you may retire.

[Exit Lady Allworth with Waiting-woman and Chambermaid.]

132Nay, all's forgotten;
133And, for a lucky omen to my project,
134Shake hands and end all quarrels in the cellar.

ORDER

135Agreed, agreed.

FURNACE

Agreed, agreed. Still merry Master Wellborn!

Exeunt.

2.1

[Enter] Overreach [and] Marall.

OVERREACH

1He's gone, I warrant thee; this commission crushed him.

MARALL

2Your Worship have the way on't, and ne'er miss
3To squeeze these unthrifts into air; and yet
4The chap-fall'n justice did his part, returning
5For your advantage the certificate,
6Against his conscience and his knowledge too
7(With your good favor), to the utter ruin
8Of the poor farmer.

OVERREACH

Of the poor farmer. 'Twas for these good ends
9I made him a justice. He that bribes his belly
10Is certain to command his soul.

MARALL

Is certain to command his soul. I wonder
11(Still with your license) why, Your Worship having
12The power to put this thin-gut in commission,
13You are not in't yourself?

OVERREACH

You are not in't yourself? Thou art a fool.
14In being out of office I am out of danger,
15Where, if I were a justice, besides the trouble,
16I might or out of willfulness or error
17Run myself finely into a praemuníre,
18And so become a prey to the informer.
19No, I'll have none of't. 'Tis enough I keep
20Greedy at my devotion; so he serve
21My purposes, let him hang, or damn, I care not.
22Friendship is but a word.

MARALL

Friendship is but a word. You are all wisdom.

OVERREACH

23I would be wordly-wise; for the other wisdom,
24That does prescribe us a well-governed life,
25And to do right to others as ourselves,
26I value not an atom.

MARALL

I value not an atom. What course take you,
27With your good patience, to hedge in the manor
28Of your neighbor Master Frugal? As 'tis said
29He will nor sell nor borrow nor exchange,
30And his land, lying in the midst of your many lordships,
31Is a foul blemish.

OVERREACH

Is a foul blemish. I have thought on't, Marrall,
32And it shall take. I must have all men sellers,
33And I the only purchaser.

MARALL

And I the only purchaser. 'Tis most fit, sir.

OVERREACH

34I'll therefore buy some cottage near his manor,
35Which done, I'll make my men break ope his fences,
36Ride o'er his standing corn, and in the night
37Set fire on his barns, or break his cattle's legs.
38These trespasses draw on suits, and suits expenses,
39Which I can spare, but will soon beggar him.
40When I have harried him thus two or three year,
41Though he sue in forma pauperis, in spite
42Of all his thrift and care he'll grow behindhand.

MARALL

43The best I ever heard! I could adore you.

OVERREACH

44Then with the favor of my man of law,
45I will pretend some title. Want will force him
46To put it to arbitrament; then, if he sell
47For half the value, he shall have ready money,
48And I possess his land.

MARALL

And I possess his land. 'Tis above wonder!
49Wellborn was apt to sell, and needed not
50These fine arts, sir, to hook him in.

OVERREACH

These fine arts, sir, to hook him in. Well thought on.
51This varlet, Marall, lives too long to upbraid me
52With my close cheat put upon him. Will nor cold
53Nor hunger kill him?

MARALL

Nor hunger kill him? I know not what to think on't.
54I have used all means, and the last night I caused
55His host the tapster to turn him out of doors,
56And have been since with all your friends and tenants,
57And on the forfeit of your favour charged 'em,
58Though a crust of moldy bread would keep him from starving,
59Yet they should not relieve him. This is done, sir.

OVERREACH

60That was something, Marall, but thou must go further,
61And suddenly, Marall.

MARALL

And suddenly, Marall. Where and when you please, sir.

OVERREACH

62I would have thee seek him out, and, if thou canst,
63Persuade him that 'tis better steal than beg.
64Then if I prove he has but robbed a henroost,
65Not all the world shall save him from the gallows.
66Do anything to work him to despair,
67And 'tis thy masterpiece.

MARALL

And 'tis thy masterpiece. I will do my best, sir.

OVERREACH

68I am now on my main work with the Lord Lovell,
69The gallant-minded, popular Lord Lovell;
70The minion of the people's love. I hear
71He's come into the country, and my aims are
72To insinuate myself into his knowledge,
73And then invite him to my house.

MARALL

And then invite him to my house. I have you.
74This points at my young mistress.

OVERREACH

This points at my young mistress. She must part with
75That humble title, and write "Honorable,"
76"Right Honorable," Marall, my "Right Honorable" daughter,
77If all I have, or e'er shall get, will do it.
78I will have her well attended; there are ladies
79Of errant knights decayed and brought so low
80That, for cast clothes and meat, will gladly serve her.
81And 'tis my glory, though I come from the city,
82To have their issue, whom I have undone,
83To kneel to mine as bondslaves.

MARALL

To kneel to mine as bondslaves. 'Tis fit state, sir.

OVERREACH

84And therefore, I'll not have a chambermaid
85That ties her shoes, or any meaner office,
86But such whose fathers were Right Worshipful.
87'Tis a rich man's pride, there having ever been
88More than a feud, a strange antipathy
89Between us and true gentry.

Enter Wellborn.

MARALL

Between us and true gentry. See who's here, sir.

OVERREACH

90Hence, monster! Prodigy!

WELLBORN

Hence, monster! Prodigy! Sir, your wife's nephew;
91She and my father tumbled in one belly.

OVERREACH

92Avoid my sight! Thy breath's infectious, rogue.
93I shun thee as a leprosy, or the plague.—
94Come hither, Marall. [aside to him] This is the time to work him.aparte

MARALL

95I warrant you, sir.

Exit Overreach.

WELLBORN

I warrant you, sir. By this light, I think he's mad.

MARALL

96Mad? Had you took compassion on yourself,
97You long since had been mad.

WELLBORN

You long since had been mad. You have took a course,
98Between you and my venerable uncle,
99To make me so.

MARALL

To make me so. The more pale-spirited you,
100That would not be instructed. I swear deeply—

WELLBORN

101By what?

MARALL

By what? By my religion.

WELLBORN

By what? By my religion. Thy religion!
102The devil's creed. But what would you have done?

MARALL

103Had there been but one tree in all the shire,
104Nor any hope to compass a penny halter,
105Before, like you, I had outlived my fortunes,
106A withe had served my turn to hang myself.
107I am zealous in your cause; pray you, hang yourself,
108And presently, as you love your credit.

WELLBORN

And presently, as you love your credit. I thank you.

MARALL

109Will you stay till you die in a ditch, or lice devour you?
110Or if you dare not do the feat yourself,
111But that you'll put the state to charge and trouble,
112Is there no purse to be cut? House to be broken?
113Or market women with eggs that you may murder,
114And so dispatch the business?

WELLBORN

And so dispatch the business? Here's variety,
115I must confess; but I'll accept of none
116Of all your gentle offers, I assure you.

MARALL

117Why, have you hope ever to eat again?
118Or drink? Or be the master of three farthings?
119If you like not hanging, drown yourself. Take some course
120For your reputation.

WELLBORN

For your reputation. 'Twill not do, dear tempter,
121With all the rhetoric the fiend hath taught you.
122I am as far as thou art from despair;
123Nay, I have confidence, which is more than hope,
124To live, and suddenly, better than ever.

MARALL

125Ha! Ha! These castles you build in the air
126Will not persuade me or to give or lend
127A token to you.

WELLBORN

A token to you. I'll be more kind to thee.
128Come, thou shalt dine with me.

MARALL

Come, thou shalt dine with me. With you?

WELLBORN

Come, thou shalt dine with me. With you? Nay, more, dine gratis.

MARALL

129Under what hedge, I pray you? Or at whose cost?
130Are they padders or Abram-men that are your consorts?

WELLBORN

131Thou art incredulous, but thou shalt dine
132Not alone at her house, but with a gallant lady—
133With me and with a lady.

MARALL

With me and with a lady. Lady? What lady?
134With the Lady of the Lake, or Queen of Fairies?
135For I know it must be an enchanted dinner.

WELLBORN

136With the Lady Allworth, knave.

MARALL

With the Lady Allworth, knave. Nay, now there's hope
137Thy brain is cracked.

WELLBORN

Thy brain is cracked. Mark there with what respect
138I am entertained.

MARALL

I am entertained. With choice, no doubt, of dog whips.
139Why, dost thou ever hope to pass her porter?

WELLBORN

140'Tis not far off; go with me. Trust thine own eyes.

MARALL

141Troth, in my hope, or my assurance rather
142To see thee curvet and mount like a dog in a blanket
143If ever thou presume to pass her threshold,
144I will endure thy company.

WELLBORN

I will endure thy company. Come along, then.

Exeunt.

2.2

[Enter] Allworth, Waiting-woman, Chambermaid, Order, Amble, Furnace, [and] Watchall.

WAITING-WOMAN

1[to Allworth] Could you not command your leisure one hour longer?

CHAMBERMAID

2Or half an hour?

ALLWORTH

Or half an hour? I have told you what my haste is.
3Besides, being now another's, not mine own,
4Howe'er I much desire to enjoy you longer,
5My duty suffers if, to please myself,
6I should neglect my lord.

WAITING-WOMAN

I should neglect my lord. Pray you do me the favor
7To put these few quince cakes into your pocket;
8They are of mine own preserving.

CHAMBERMAID

They are of mine own preserving. And this marmalade;
9'Tis comfortable for your stomach.

WAITING-WOMAN

'Tis comfortable for your stomach. And, at parting,
10Excuse me if I beg a farewell from you.

CHAMBERMAID

11[to her] You are still before me.—I move the same suit, sir.

[Allworth] kisses 'em severally.

FURNACE

12How greedy these chamberers are of a beardless chin!
13I think the tits will ravish him.

ALLWORTH

I think the tits will ravish him. My service
14To both.

WAITING-WOMAN

To both. Ours waits on you.

CHAMBERMAID

To both. Ours waits on you. And shall do ever.

ORDER

15[to the women] You hear my lady's charge; be therefore careful
16That you sustain your parts.

WAITING-WOMAN

That you sustain your parts. We can bear, I warrant you.

Exeunt [Waiting-]woman and Chambermaid.

FURNACE

17[to Allworth] Here; drink it off. The ingredients are cordial,
18And this the true elixir; it hath boiled
19Since midnight for you. 'Tis the quintessence
20Of five cocks of the game, ten dozen of sparrows,
21Knuckles of veal, potato roots, and marrow,
22Coral, and ambergris. Were you two years elder,
23And I had a wife or gamesome mistress,
24I durst trust you with neither. You need not bait
25After this, I warrant you; though your journey's long,
26You may ride on the strength of this till tomorrow morning.

ALLWORTH

27Your courtesies overwhelm me. I much grieve
28To part from such true friends, and yet find comfort;
29My attendance on my honorable lord,
30Whose resolution holds to visit my lady,
31Will speedily bring me back.

Knocking at the gate; Marall and Wellborn [speak] within.

MARALL

Will speedily bring me back. [within] Dar'st thou venture further?

WELLBORN

32[within] Yes, yes, and knock again.

ORDER

[within] Yes, yes, and knock again. [to the others] 'Tis he! Disperse.

AMBLE

33[to the others] Perform it bravely.

FURNACE

[to the others] Perform it bravely. I know my cue. Ne'er doubt me.

They go off several ways. [Allworth remains onstage.]

[Enter Watchall with Wellborn and Marall.]

WATCHALL

34[to Wellborn] Beast that I was, to make you stay! Most welcome.
35You were long since expected.

WELLBORN

You were long since expected. Say so much
36To my friend, I pray you.

WATCHALL

To my friend, I pray you. For your sake I will, sir.

MARALL

37[aside] For his sake!aparte

WELLBORN

[aside] For his sake! [aside to Marall] Mum! This is nothing.aparte

MARALL

[aside] For his sake! [aside to Marall] Mum! This is nothing. [aside] More than everaparte
38I would have believed, though I had found it in my primer.

ALLWORTH

39When I have giv'n you reasons for my late harshness,
40You'll pardon and excuse me, for, believe me,
41Though now I part abruptly, in my service
42I will deserve it.

MARALL

I will deserve it. [aside] Service! With a vengeance!aparte

WELLBORN

43I am satisfied. Farewell, Tom.

ALLWORTH

I am satisfied. Farewell, Tom. All joy stay with you!

Exit Allworth.

Enter Amble.

AMBLE

44[to Wellborn] You are happily encountered! I yet never
45Presented one so welcome as I know
46You will be to my lady.

MARALL

You will be to my lady. [aside] This is some vision,aparte
47Or, sure, these men are mad, to worship a dunghill.
48It cannot be a truth.

WELLBORN

It cannot be a truth. [aside to Marall] Be still a pagan,aparte
49An unbelieving infidel; be so, miscreant,
50And meditate on blankets and on dog whips!

Enter Furnace.

FURNACE

51[to Wellborn] I am glad you are come. Until I know your pleasure,
52I knew not how to serve up my lady's dinner.

MARALL

53[aside] His pleasure! Is it possible?aparte

WELLBORN

[aside] His pleasure! Is it possible? [to Furnace] What's thy will?

FURNACE

54Marry, sir, I have some grouse, and turkey chicken,
55Some rails, and quails, and my lady willed me ask you
56What kind of sauces best affect your palate,
57That I may use my utmost skill to please it.

[Wellborn and Furnace confer privately.]

MARALL

58[aside] The devil's entered this cook. Sauce for his palate,aparte
59That, on my knowledge, for almost this twelvemonth
60Durst wish but cheese parings and brown bread on Sundays!

WELLBORN

61[to Furnace] That way I like 'em best.

FURNACE

[to Furnace] That way I like 'em best. It shall be done, sir.

Exit Furnace.

WELLBORN

62[aside to Marall] What think you of the hedge we shall dine under?aparte
63Shall we feed gratis?

MARALL

Shall we feed gratis? I know not what to think.
64Pray you, make me not mad.

Enter Order.

ORDER

Pray you, make me not mad. [to Wellborn] This place becomes you not.
65Pray you, walk, sir, to the dining room.

WELLBORN

Pray you, walk, sir, to the dining room. I am well here
66Till Her Ladyship quits her chamber.

MARALL

Till Her Ladyship quits her chamber. [aside] "Well here," say you?aparte
67'Tis a rare change! But yesterday you thought
68Yourself well in a barn, wrapped up in peas straw.

Enter [Waiting-]woman and Chambermaid.

WAITING-WOMAN

69[to Wellborn] Oh, sir, you are wished for.

CHAMBERMAID

[to Wellborn] Oh, sir, you are wished for. [to Wellborn] My lady dreamt, sir, of you.

WAITING-WOMAN

70And the first command she gave after she rose
71Was (her devotions done) to give her notice
72When you approached here.

CHAMBERMAID

When you approached here. Which is done, on my virtue.

MARALL

73[aside] I shall be converted. I begin to growaparte
74Into a new belief, which saints nor angels
75Could have won me to have faith in.

WAITING-WOMAN

Could have won me to have faith in. Sir, my lady!

Enter Lady [Allworth].

LADY ALLWORTH

76I come to meet you, and languished till I saw you.
77This first kiss is for form; I allow a second
78To such a friend.

[She kisses Wellborn warmly.]

MARALL

To such a friend. [aside] To such a friend! Heav'n bless me!aparte

WELLBORN

79I am wholly yours; yet, madam, if you please
80To grace this gentleman with a salute—

MARALL

81[aside] Salute me at his bidding!aparte

WELLBORN

[aside] Salute me at his bidding! I shall receive it
82As a most high favor.

LADY ALLWORTH

As a most high favor. Sir, you may command me.

[She offers to kiss Marall, who draws back.]

WELLBORN

83Run backward from a lady? And such a lady?

MARALL

84To kiss her foot is, to poor me, a favor
85I am unworthy of—

[He kneels and] offers to kiss her foot.

LADY ALLWORTH

I am unworthy of— Nay, pray you, rise,
86And, since you are so humble, I'll exalt you.
87You shall dine with me today at mine own table.

MARALL

88Your Ladyship's table? I am not good enough
89To sit at your steward's board.

LADY ALLWORTH

To sit at your steward's board. You are too modest.
90I will not be denied.

Enter Furnace.

FURNACE

I will not be denied. Will you still be babbling
91Till your meat freeze on the table? The old trick still;
92My art ne'er thought on!

LADY ALLWORTH

My art ne'er thought on! Your arm, Master Wellborn.
93[To Marall] Nay, keeps us company.

MARALL

[To Marall] Nay, keeps us company. I was never so graced.

Exeunt Wellborn, Lady [Allworth], Amble, Marall, [Waiting-]woman, [and Chambermaid].

ORDER

94So, we have played our parts, and are come off well.
95But if know the mystery, why my lady
96Consented to it, or why Master Wellborn
97Desired it, may I perish!

FURNACE

Desired it, may I perish! Would I had
98The roasting of his heart that cheated him
99And forces the poor gentleman to these shifts!
100By fire (for cooks are Persians, and swear by it),
101Of all the griping and extorting tyrants
102I ever heard or read of, I ne'er met
103A match to Sir Giles Overreach.

WATCHALL

A match to Sir Giles Overreach. What will you take
104To tell him so, fellow Furnace?

FURNACE

To tell him so, fellow Furnace? Just as much
105As my throat is worth, for that would be the price on't.
106To have a usurer that starves himself,
107And wears a cloak of one-and-twenty years
108On a suit of fourteen groats, bought of the hangman,
109To grow rich, and then purchase, is too common;
110But this Sir Giles feeds high, keeps many servants,
111Who must at his command do any outrage.
112Rich in his habit, vast in his expenses,
113Yet he to admiration still increases
114In wealth and lordships.

ORDER

In wealth and lordships. He frights men out of their estates,
115And breaks through all law nets made to curb ill men
116As they were cobwebs. No man dares reprove him.
117Such a spirit to dare and power to do were never
118Lodged so unluckily.

Enter Amble.

AMBLE

Lodged so unluckily. Ha, ha! I shall burst.

ORDER

119Contain thyself, man.

FURNACE

Contain thyself, man. Or make us partakers
120Of your sudden mirth.

AMBLE

Of your sudden mirth. Ha, ha! My lady has got
121Such a guest at her table—this term driver, Marrall,
122This snip of an attorney!

FURNACE

This snip of an attorney! What of him, man?

AMBLE

123The knave thinks still he's at the cook's shop in Ram Alley,
124Where the clerks divide, and the elder is to choose;
125And feeds so slovenly!

FURNACE

And feeds so slovenly! Is this all?

AMBLE

And feeds so slovenly! Is this all? My lady
126Drank to him for fashion sake, or to please Master Wellborn.
127As I live, he rises, and takes up a dish
128In which there were some remnants of a boiled capon,
129And pledges her in white broth!

FURNACE

And pledges her in white broth! Nay, 'tis like
130The rest of his tribe.

AMBLE

The rest of his tribe. And when I brought him wine,
131He leaves his stool, and after a leg or two
132Most humbly thanks My Worship.

ORDER

Most humbly thanks My Worship. Rose already!

AMBLE

133I shall be chid.

Enter Lady [Allworth], Wellborn, [and] Marrall.

FURNACE

I shall be chid. [aside] My lady frowns.aparte

LADY ALLWORTH

I shall be chid. [aside] My lady frowns. [to Amble] You wait well!
134Let me have no more of this. I observed your jeering.
135Sirrah, I'll have you know, whom I think worthy
136To sit at my table, be he ne'er so mean,
137When I am present, is not your companion.

ORDER

138[aside] Nay, she'll preserve what's due to her.aparte

FURNACE

[aside] Nay, she'll preserve what's due to her. [aside to Amble] This refreshingaparte
139Follows your flux of laughter.

LADY ALLWORTH

Follows your flux of laughter. [To Wellborn.] You are master
140Of your own will. I know so much of manners
141As not to inquire your purposes. In a word,
142To me you are ever welcome as to a house
143That is your own.

WELLBORN

That is your own. [aside to Marall] Mark that!aparte

MARALL

That is your own. [aside to Marall] Mark that! [aside to Wellborn] With reverence, sir,aparte
144An it like Your Worship.

WELLBORN

An it like Your Worship. Trouble yourself no farther,
145Dear madam. My heart's full of zeal and service,
146However in my language I am sparing.—
147Come, Master Marrall.

MARALL

Come, Master Marrall. I attend Your Worship.

Exeunt Wellborn [and] Marall.

LADY ALLWORTH

148I see in your looks you are sorry, and you know me
149An easy mistress. Be merry; I have forgot all.—
150Order and Furnace, come with me; I must give you
151Further directions.

ORDER

Further directions. What you please.

FURNACE

Further directions. What you please. We are ready.

[Exeunt.]

2.3

[Enter] Wellborn [and] Marall.

WELLBORN

1I think I am in a good way.

MARALL

I think I am in a good way. Good sir, the best way,
2The certain best way.

WELLBORN

The certain best way. There are casualties
3That men are subject to.

MARALL

That men are subject to. You are above 'em;
4And, as you are already Worshipful,
5I hope ere long you will increase in worship
6And be Right Worshipful.

WELLBORN

And be Right Worshipful. Prithee, do not flout me.
7What I shall be, I shall be. Is't for your ease
8You keep your hat off?

MARALL

You keep your hat off? Ease, an it like Your Worship?
9I hope Jack Marrall shall not live so long
10To prove himself such an unmannerly beast,
11Though it hail hazelnuts, as to be covered
12When Your Worship's present.

WELLBORN

When Your Worship's present. (aside) Is not this a true rogue?aparte
13That, out of mere hope of a future cos'nage,
14Can turn thus suddenly? 'Tis rank already.

MARALL

15I know Your Worship's wise, and needs no counsel;
16Yet if, in my desire to do you service,
17I humbly offer my advice (but still
18Under correction), I hope I shall not
19Incur your high displeasure.

WELLBORN

Incur your high displeasure. No. Speak freely.

MARALL

20Then, in my judgment, sir, my simple judgment
21(Still with Your Worship's favor), I could wish you
22A better habit, for this cannot be
23But much distasteful to the noble lady
24(I say no more) that loves you; for, this morning
25To me (and I am but a swine to her),
26Before th'assurance of her wealth perfumed you,
27You savored not of amber.

WELLBORN

You savored not of amber. I do now, then?

[Marall] kisses the end of his [Wellborn's] cudgel.

MARALL

28This your baton hath got a touch of it.
29Yet, if your please, for change I have twenty pounds here,
30Which, out of my true love, I presently
31Lay down at Your Worship's feet. 'Twill serve to buy you
32A riding suit.

[He offers money.]

WELLBORN

A riding suit. But where's the horse?

MARALL

A riding suit. But where's the horse? My gelding
33Is at your service; nay, you shall ride me
34Before Your Worship shall be put to the trouble
35To walk afoot. Alas, when you are lord
36Of this lady's manor, as I know you will be,
37You may, with the lease of glebe land called Knave's Acre—
38A place I would manure—requite your vassal.

WELLBORN

39I thank thy love, but must make no use of it.
40What's twenty pounds?

MARALL

What's twenty pounds? 'Tis all that I can make, sir.

WELLBORN

41Dost thou think, though I want clothes I could not have 'em
42For one word to my lady?

MARALL

For one word to my lady? As I know not that!

WELLBORN

43Come, I'll tell thee a secret, and so leave thee.
44I'll not give her the advantage, though she be
45A gallant-minded lady, after we are married
46(There being no woman but is sometimes froward)
47To hit me in the teeth and say she was forced
48To buy my wedding clothes, and took me on
49With a plain riding suit and an ambling nag.
50No, I'll be furnished something like myself.
51And so farewell. For thy suit touching Knave's Acre,
52When it is mine, 'tis thine.

MARALL

When it is mine, 'tis thine. I thank Your Worship.

Exit Wellborn.

53How I was cozened in the calculation
54Of this man's fortune! My master cozened too,
55Whose pupil I am in the art of undoing men,
56For that is our profession. Well, well, Master Wellborn,
57You are of a sweet nature, and fit again to be cheated—
58Which, if the Fates please, when you are possessed
59Of the land and lady, you, sans question, shall be.
60I'll presently think of the means.

Walks by, musing.

Enter Overreach.

OVERREACH

I'll presently think of the means. [to a servant within] Sirrah, take my horse.
61I'll walk to get me an appetite. 'Tis but a mile,
62And exercise will keep me from being pursy.—
63Ha! Marrall! Is he conjuring? Perhaps
64The knave has wrought the prodigal to do
65Some outrage on himself, and now he feels
66Compunction in his conscience for't. No matter,
67So it be done.—Marrall!

MARALL

So it be done.—Marrall! Sir?

OVERREACH

So it be done.—Marrall! Sir? How succeed we
68In our plot on Wellborn?

MARALL

In our plot on Wellborn? Never better, sir.

OVERREACH

69Has he hanged or drowned himself?

MARALL

Has he hanged or drowned himself? No, sir, he lives—
70Lives once more to be made a prey to you,
71A greater prey than ever.

OVERREACH

A greater prey than ever. Art thou in thy wits?
72If thou art, reveal this miracle, and briefly.

MARALL

73A lady, sir, is fall'n in love with him.

OVERREACH

74With him? What lady?

MARALL

With him? What lady? The rich Lady Allworth.

OVERREACH

75Thou dolt! How dar'st thou speak this?

MARALL

Thou dolt! How dar'st thou speak this? I speak truth;
76And I do so but once a year, unless
77It be to you, sir. We dined with Her Ladyship,
78I thank His Worship.

OVERREACH

I thank His Worship. His Worship!

MARALL

I thank His Worship. His Worship! As I live, sir,
79I dined with him at the great lady's table,
80Simple as I stand here, and saw when she kissed him,
81And would at his request have kissed me too,
82But I was not so audacious as some youths are
83And dare do anything, be it ne'er so absurd,
84And sad after performance.

OVERREACH

And sad after performance. Why, thou rascal,
85To tell me these impossibilities!
86Dine at her table? And kiss him? Or thee?
87Impudent varlet! Have not I myself,
88To whom great countesses' doors have oft flew open,
89Ten times attempted, since her husband's death,
90In vain to see her, though I came—a suitor?
91And yet Your good Solicitorship and rogue Wellborn
92Were brought into her presence, feasted with her!
93But that I know thee a dog, that cannot blush,
94This most incredible lie would call up one
95On thy buttermilk cheeks.

MARALL

On thy buttermilk cheeks. Shall I not trust my eyes, sir?
96Or taste? I feel her good cheer in my belly.

OVERREACH

97You shall feel me, if you give not over, sirrah.
98Recover your brains again, and be no more gulled
99With a beggar's plot, assisted by the aids
100Of servingmen and chambermaids—for beyond these
101Thou never saw'st a woman—or I'll quit you
102From my employments.

MARALL

From my employments. Will you credit this yet?
103On my confidence of their marriage, I offered Wellborn
104(Aside) I would give a crown now I durst say "His Worship" —aparte
105My nag and twenty pounds.

OVERREACH

My nag and twenty pounds. Did you so, idiot?

Strikes him down.

106Was this the way to work him to despair,
107Or rather to cross me?

MARALL

Or rather to cross me? Will Your Worship kill me?

OVERREACH

108No, no; but drive the lying spirit out of you.

MARALL

109He's gone.

OVERREACH

He's gone. I have done, then. Now, forgetting
110Your late imaginery feast and lady,
111Know my Lord Lovell dines with me tomorrow.
112Be careful naught be wanting to receive him,
113And bid my daughter's women trim her up;
114Though they paint her, so she catch the lord, I'll thank 'em.
115There's a piece for my late blows.

[He gives money.]

MARALL

There's a piece for my late blows. (aside) I must yet suffer:aparte
116But there may be a time—

OVERREACH

But there may be a time— Do you grumble?

MARALL

But there may be a time— Do you grumble? No, sir.

[Exeunt.]

3.1

[Enter] Lovell, Allworth, [and] servants.

LOVELL

1Walk the horses down the hill. Something in private
2I must impart to Allworth.

Exeunt servii.

ALLWORTH

I must impart to Allworth. O my lord,
3What sacrifice of reverence, duty, watching,
4Although I could put off the use of sleep
5And ever wait on your commands to serve 'em,
6What dangers, though in ne'er so horrid shapes,
7Nay, death itself, though I should run to meet it,
8Can I, and with a thankful willingness, suffer,
9But still the retribution will fall short
10Of your bounties show'red upon me!

LOVELL

Of your bounties show'red upon me! Loving youth,
11Till what I purpose be put into act,
12Do not o'erprize it. Since you have trusted me
13With your soul's nearest—nay, her dearest—secret,
14Rest confident 'tis in a cabinet locked
15Treachery shall never open. I have found you
16(For so much to your face I must profess,
17Howe'er you guard your modesty with a blush for't)
18More zealous in your love and service to me
19Than I have been in my rewards.

ALLWORTH

Than I have been in my rewards. Still great ones,
20Above my merit.

LOVELL

Above my merit. Such your gratitude calls 'em;
21Nor am I of that harsh and rugged temper
22As some great men are taxed with, who imagine
23They part from the respect due to their honors
24If they use not all such as follow 'em,
25Without distinction of their births, like slaves.
26I am not so conditioned. I can make
27A fitting difference between my footboy
28And a gentleman by want compelled to serve me.

ALLWORTH

29'Tis thankfully acknowledged. You have been
30More like a father to me than a master.
31Pray you, pardon the comparison.

LOVELL

Pray you, pardon the comparison. I allow it;
32And, to give you assurance I am pleased in't,
33My carriage and demeanor to your mistress,
34Fair Margaret, shall truly witness for me
35I can command my passions.

ALLWORTH

I can command my passions. 'Tis a conquest
36Few lords can boast of when they are tempted.—Oh!

LOVELL

37Why do you sigh? Can you be doubtful of me?
38By that fair name I in the wars have purchased,
39And all my actions hitherto untainted,
40I will not be more true to mine own honor
41Than to my Allworth.

ALLWORTH

Than to my Allworth. As you are the brave Lord Lovell,
42Your bare word only given is an assurance
43Of more validity and weight to me
44Than all the oaths bound up with imprecations
45Which, when they would deceive, most courtiers practice.
46Yet, being a man (for, sure, to style you more
47Would relish of gross flattery), I am forced,
48Against my confidence of your worth and virtues,
49To doubt—nay, more—to fear.

LOVELL

To doubt—nay, more—to fear. So young, and jealous?

ALLWORTH

50Were you to encounter with a single foe,
51The victory were certain; but to stand
52The charge of two such potent enemies,
53At once assaulting you, as wealth and beauty,
54And those too seconded with power, is odds
55Too great for Hercules.

LOVELL

Too great for Hercules. Speak your doubts and fears,
56Since you will nourish 'em, in plainer language,
57That I may understand 'em.

ALLWORTH

That I may understand 'em. What's your will,
58Though I lend arms against myself (provided
59They may advantage you) must be obeyed.
60My much loved lord, were Margaret only fair,
61The cannon of her more than earthly form,
62Though mounted high, commanding all beneath it,
63And rammed with bullets of her sparkling eyes,
64Of all the bulwarks that defend your senses
65Could batter none but that which guards your sight.
66But when the well-tuned accents of her tongue
67Make music to you, and with numerous sounds
68Assault your hearing (such as if Ulysses
69Now lived again, howe'er he stood the Sirens,
70Could not resist), the combat must grow doubtful
71Between your reason and rebellious passions.
72Add this too; when you feel her touch and breath,
73Like a soft western wind when it glides o'er
74Arabia creating gums and spices,
75And, in the van, the nectar of her lips
76Which you must taste, bring the battalia on,
77Well armed, and strongly lined with her discourse
78And knowing manners, to give entertainment—
79Hippolytus himself would leave Diana
80To follow such a Venus.

LOVELL

To follow such a Venus. Love hath made you
81Poetical, Allworth.

ALLWORTH

Poetical, Allworth. Grant all these beat off
82(Which, if it be in man to do, you'll do it),
83Mammon, in Sir Giles Overreach, steps in
84With heaps of ill-got gold, and so much land,
85To make her more remarkable, as would tire
86A falcon's wings in one day to fly over.
87O my good lord, these powerful aids, which would
88Make a misshapen Negro beautiful
89(Yet are but ornaments to give her lustre
90That in herself is all perfection), must
91Prevail for her. I here release your trust.
92'Tis happiness enough for me to serve you
93And sometimes with chaste eyes to look upon her.

LOVELL

94Why, shall I swear?

ALLWORTH

Why, shall I swear? Oh, by no means, my lord;
95And wrong not so your judgment to the world
96As from your fond indulgence to a boy,
97Your page, your servant, to refuse a blessing
98Divers great men are rivals for.

LOVELL

Divers great men are rivals for. Suspend
99Your judgment till the trial. How far is it
100T'Overreach's house?

ALLWORTH

T'Overreach's house? At the most, some half hour's riding;
101You'll soon be there.

LOVELL

You'll soon be there. And you the sooner freed
102From your jealous fears.

ALLWORTH

From your jealous fears. Oh, that I durst but hope it!

Exeunt.

3.2

[Enter] Overreach, Greedy, [and] Marall.

OVERREACH

1Spare for no cost. Let my dressers crack with the weight
2Of curious viands.

GREEDY

Of curious viands. Store indeed's no sore, sir.

OVERREACH

3That proverb fits your stomach, Master Greedy.
4And let no plate be seen but what's pure gold,
5Or such whose workmanship exceeds the matter
6That it is made of. Let my choicest linen
7Perfume the room, and, when we wash, the water,
8With precious powders mixed, so please my lord
9That he may with envy wish to bathe so ever.

MARALL

10'Twill be very chargeable.

OVERREACH

'Twill be very chargeable. Avaunt, you drudge!
11Now all my labored ends are at the stake,
12It's a time to think of thrift? Call in my daughter.

[Exit Marall.]

13And, Master Justice, since you love choice dishes,
14And plenty of 'em—

GREEDY

And plenty of 'em— As I do indeed, sir,
15Almost as much as to give thanks for 'em.

OVERREACH

16I do confer that providence, with my power
17Of absolute command to have abundance,
18To your best care.

GREEDY

To your best care. I'll punctually discharge it
19And give the best directions. Now am I
20In mine own conceit a monarch, at the least
21Archpresident of the boiled, the roast, the baked,
22For which I will eat often, and give thanks,
23When my belly's braced up like a drum—and that's pure justice.

Exit Greedy.

OVERREACH

24It must be so. Should the foolish girl prove modest,
25She may spoil all. She had it not from me,
26But from her mother. I was ever forward,
27As she must be, and therefore I'll prepare her.

[Enter] Margaret.

28Alone—and let your women wait without.

MARGARET

29Your pleasure, sir?

OVERREACH

Your pleasure, sir? Ha, this is a neat dressing!
30These orient pearls, and diamonds well placed too!
31The gown affects me not; it should have been
32Embroidered o'er and o'er with flowers of gold;
33But these rich jewels and quaint fashion help it.
34And how below? Since oft the wanton eye,
35The face observed, descends unto the foot,
36Which, being well proportioned, as yours is,
37Invites as much as perfect white and red,
38Though without art. How like you your new woman,
39The Lady Downfall'n?

MARGARET

The Lady Downfall'n? Well, for a companion;
40Not as a servant.

OVERREACH

Not as a servant. Is she humble, Meg?
41And careful too, her ladyship forgotten?

MARGARET

42I pity her fortune.

OVERREACH

I pity her fortune. Pity her? Trample on her!
43I took her up in an old tamin gown,
44(Even starved for want of twopenny chops) to serve thee;
45And if I understand she but repines
46To do thee any duty, though ne'er so servile,
47I'll pack her to her knight, where I have lodged him,
48Into the Counter, and there let 'em howl together.

MARGARET

49You know your own ways; but, for me, I blush
50When I command her that was once attended
51With persons not inferior to myself
52In birth.

OVERREACH

In birth. In birth? Why, art thou not my daughter?
53The blest child of my industry and wealth?
54Why, foolish girl, was't not to make thee great
55That I have ran, and still pursue, those ways
56That hale down curses on me, which I mind not?
57Part with these humble thoughts, and apt thyself
58To the noble state I labor to advance thee,
59Or, by my hopes to see thee "Honorable,"
60I will adopt a stranger to my heir
61And throw thee from my care. Do not provoke me.

MARGARET

62I will not, sir. Mold me which way you please.

Enter Greedy.

OVERREACH

63How! Interrupted?

GREEDY

How! Interrupted? 'Tis matter of importance.
64The cook, sir, is self-willed and will not learn
65From my experience. There's a fawn brought in, sir,
66And, for my life, I cannot make him roast it
67With a Norfolk dumpling in the belly of it.
68And, sir, we wise men know, without the dumpling
69'Tis not worth threepence.

OVERREACH

'Tis not worth threepence. Would it were whole in thy belly
70To stuff it out! Cook it any way. Prithee leave me.

GREEDY

71Without order for the dumpling?

OVERREACH

Without order for the dumpling? Let it be dumpled
72Which way thou wilt, or tell him I will scald him
73In his own cauldron.

GREEDY

In his own cauldron. I had lost my stomach,
74Had I lost my Mistress Dumpling I'll give thanks for.

Exit Greedy.

OVERREACH

75But to our business, Meg. You have heard who dines here?

MARGARET

76I have, sir.

OVERREACH

I have, sir. 'Tis an honorable man,
77A lord, Meg, and commands a regiment
78Of soldiers, and, what's rare, is one himself,
79A bold and understanding one; and to be
80A lord and a good leader in one volume
81Is granted unto few but such as rise up
82The kingdom's glory.

Enter Greedy.

GREEDY

The kingdom's glory. I'll resign my office
83If I be not better obeyed.

OVERREACH

If I be not better obeyed. 'Slight, art thou frantic?

GREEDY

84Frantic? 'Twould make me a frantic, and stark mad,
85Were I not a Justice of Peace, and Coram too,
86Which this rebellious cook cares not a straw for.
87There are a dozen of woodcocks—

OVERREACH

There are a dozen of woodcocks— Make thyself
88Thirteen, the baker's dozen.

GREEDY

Thirteen, the baker's dozen. I am contented,
89So they may be dressed to my mind. He has found out
90A new device for sauce, and will not dish 'em
91With toasts and butter. My father was a tailor,
92And my name, though a justice, Greedy Woodcock;
93And ere I'll see my lineage so abused,
94I'll give up my commission.

OVERREACH

I'll give up my commission. [to the cook within] Cook! Rogue, obey him!
95[To Greedy] I have given the word; pray you, now remove yourself
96To a collar of brawn, and trouble me no farther.

GREEDY

97I will, and meditate what to eat at dinner.

Exit Greedy.

OVERREACH

98And as I said, Meg, when this gull disturbed us,
99This honorable lord, this colonel,
100I would have thy husband.

MARGARET

I would have thy husband. There's too much disparity
101Between his quality and mine to hope it.

OVERREACH

102I more than hope't, and doubt not to effect it.
103Be thou no enemy to thyself; my wealth
104Shall weigh his titles down, and make you equals.
105Now for the means to assure him thine. Observe me:
106Remember he's a courtier and a soldier
107And not to be trifled with, and therefore when
108He comes to woo you, see you do not coy it.
109This mincing modesty hath spoiled many a match
110By a first refusal, in vain after hoped for.

MARGARET

111You'll have me, sir, preserve the distance that
112Confines a virgin?

OVERREACH

Confines a virgin? Virgin me no virgins!
113I must have you lose that name, or you lose me.
114I will have you private—start not—I say, private.
115If thou art my true daughter, not a bastard,
116Thou wilt venture alone with one man, though he came
117Like Jupiter to Semele, and come off too;
118And therefore when he kisses you, kiss close.

MARGARET

119I have heard this is the strumpet's fashion, sir,
120Which I must never learn.

OVERREACH

Which I must never learn. Learn anything,
121And from any creature that may make thee great—
122From the devil himself.

MARGARET

From the devil himself. This is but devilish doctrine.

OVERREACH

123Or if his blood grow hot, suppose he offer
124Beyond this, do not you stay till it cool,
125But meet his ardor; if a couch be near,
126Sit down on't, and invite him.

MARGARET

Sit down on't, and invite him. In your house?
127Your own house, sir? For heav'n's sake, what are you then?
128Or what shall I be, sir?

OVERREACH

Or what shall I be, sir? Stand not on form.
129Words are no substances.

MARGARET

Words are no substances. Though you could dispense
130With your own honor, cast aside religion,
131The hopes of heaven or fear of hell, excuse me
132In worldly policy, this is not the way
133To make me his wife; his whore, I grant it may do.
134My maiden honor so soon yielded up,
135Nay, prostituted, cannot but assure him
136I that am light to him will not hold weight
137When he is tempted by others; so, in judgment,
138When to his lust I have given up my honor,
139He must and will forsake me.

OVERREACH

He must and will forsake me. How? Forsake thee?
140Do I wear a sword for fashion? Or is this arm
141Shrunk up? Or withered? Does there live a man
142Of that large list I have encountered with
143Can truly say I e'er gave inch of ground
144Not purchased with his blood that did oppose me?
145Forsake thee when the thing is done? He dares not.
146Give me but proof he has enjoyed thy person,
147Though all his captains, echoes to his will,
148Stood armed by his side to justify the wrong,
149And he himself in the head of his bold troop,
150Spite of his lordship and his colonelship,
151Or the judge's favor, I will make him render
152A bloody and a strict account, and force him,
153By marrying thee, to cure thy wounded honor.
154I have said it.

Enter Marall.

MARALL

I have said it. Sir, the man of honor's come
155Newly alighted.

OVERREACH

Newly alighted. [to Margaret] In, without reply,
156And do as I command, or thou art lost.

Exit Margaret.

157Is the loud music I gave order for
158Ready to receive him?

MARALL

Ready to receive him? 'Tis, sir.

OVERREACH

Ready to receive him? 'Tis, sir. Let 'em sound
159A princely welcome.

[Exit Marall.]

A princely welcome. [To himself] Roughness, awhile leave me,
160For fawning now—a stranger to my nature—
161Must make way for me.

Loud music.

Enter Lovell, Greedy, Allworth, [and] Marall.

LOVELL

Must make way for me. Sir, you meet your trouble.

OVERREACH

162What you are pleased to style so is an honor
163Above my worth and fortunes.

ALLWORTH

Above my worth and fortunes. [aside] Strange. So humble!aparte

OVERREACH

164A justice of peace, my lord.

Presents Greedy to him.

LOVELL

A justice of peace, my lord. [to Greedy] Your hand, good sir.

GREEDY

165[aside] This is a lord, and some think this a favor;aparte
166But I had rather have my hand in my dumpling.

OVERREACH

167Room for my lord!

LOVELL

Room for my lord! I miss, sir, your fair daughter
168To crown my welcome.

OVERREACH

To crown my welcome. May it please my lord
169To taste a glass of Greek wine first, and suddenly
170She shall attend my lord.

LOVELL

She shall attend my lord. You'll be obeyed, sir.

Exeunt omnes praeter Overreach.

OVERREACH

171'Tis to my wish. As soon as come, ask for her!—
172[Calling] Why, Meg! Meg Overreach!

[Enter Margaret.]

[Calling] Why, Meg! Meg Overreach! How! Tears in your eyes?
173Ha! Dry 'em quickly, or I'll dig 'em out.
174Is this a time to whimper? Meet that greatness
175That flies into thy bosom! Think what 'tis
176For me to say, "My honorable daughter,"
177And thou, when I stand bare, to say "Put on,"
178Or, "Father, you forget yourself." No more,
179But be instructed, or expect—He comes!

Enter Lovell, Greedy, Allworth, [and] Marall. They salute.

180A black-browed girl, my lord,

LOVELL

A black-browed girl, my lord, [kissing Margaret] As I live, a rare one.

ALLWORTH

181[aside.] He's took already! I am lost.aparte

OVERREACH

[aside.] He's took already! I am lost. [aside.] That kissaparte
182Came twanging off; I like it. [To the others] Quit the room!

The rest [Greedy, Allworth, and Marall, go] off.

183A little bashful, my good lord, but you,
184I hope, will teach her boldness.

LOVELL

I hope, will teach her boldness. I am happy
185In such a scholar, but—

OVERREACH

In such a scholar, but— I am past learning,
186And therefore leave you to yourselves.
And therefore leave you to yourselves. (To his daughter) Remember!

Exit Overreach.

LOVELL

187You see, fair lady, your father is solicitous
188To have you change the barren name of virgin
189Into a hopeful wife.

MARGARET

Into a hopeful wife. His haste, my lord,
190Holds no power o'er my will.

LOVELL

Holds no power o'er my will. But o'er your duty.

MARGARET

191Which, forced too much, may break.

LOVELL

Which, forced too much, may break. Bend rather, sweetest.
192Think of your years.

MARGARET

Think of your years. Too few to match with yours;
193And choicest fruits, too soon plucked, rot and wither.

LOVELL

194Do you think I am old?

MARGARET

Do you think I am old? I am sure I am too young.

LOVELL

195I can advance you.

MARGARET

I can advance you. To a hill of sorrow,
196Where every hour I may expect to fall,
197But never hope firm footing. You are noble,
198I of a low descent, however rich;
199And tissues matched with scarlet suit but ill.
200O my good lord, I could say more, but that
201I dare not trust these walls.

LOVELL

I dare not trust these walls. Pray you, trust my ear, then.

[They whisper.]

Enter Overreach, listening.

OVERREACH

202Close at it! Whispering! This is excellent!
203And, by their postures, a consent on both parts.

Enter Greedy. [He and Overreach converse, unnoticed at first by Lovell and Margaret.]

GREEDY

204Sir Giles, Sir Giles!

OVERREACH

Sir Giles, Sir Giles! The great fiend stop that clapper!

GREEDY

205It must ring out, sir, when my belly rings noon.
206The baked meats are run out, the roasts turned powder.

OVERREACH

207I shall powder you.

GREEDY

I shall powder you. Beat me to dust, I care not;
208In such a cause as this, I'll die a martyr.

OVERREACH

209Marry, and shall, you barathrum of the shambles!

Strikes him.

GREEDY

210How! Strike a justice of peace? 'Tis petty treason,
211Edwardi quinto. But that you are my friend,
212I could commit you without bail or mainprize.

OVERREACH

213Leave your bawling, sir, or I shall commit you
214Where you shall not dine today. Disturb my lord
215When he is in discourse?

GREEDY

When he is in discourse? Is't a time to talk
216When we should be munching?

LOVELL

When we should be munching? [hearing something] Ha! I heard some noise.

OVERREACH

217[privately to Greedy] Mum, villain, vanish! Shall we break a bargain
218Almost made up?

Thrust Greedy off [exiting with him].

LOVELL

Almost made up? Lady, I understand you,
219And rest most happy in your choice, believe it;
220I'll be a careful pilot to direct
221Your yet uncertain bark to a port of safety.

MARGARET

222So shall Your Honor save two lives, and bind us
223Your slaves forever.

LOVELL

Your slaves forever. I am in the act rewarded,
224Since it is good; howe'er, you must put on
225An amorous carriage towards me to delude
226Your subtle father.

MARGARET

Your subtle father. I am prone to that.

LOVELL

227Now break we off our conference.—Sir Giles!
228Where is Sir Giles?

Enter Overreach and the rest [Greedy, Marall, and Allworth].

OVERREACH

Where is Sir Giles? My noble lord! And how
229Does Your Lordship find her?

LOVELL

Does Your Lordship find her? Apt, Sir Giles, and coming,
230And I like her the better.

OVERREACH

And I like her the better. So do I too.

LOVELL

231Yet, should we take forts at the first assault,
232'Twere poor in the defendant. I must confirm her
233With a love letter or two, which I must have
234Delivered by my page, and you give way to't.

OVERREACH

235With all my soul! A towardly gentleman.—
236Your hand, good Master Allworth. Know my house
237Is ever open to you.

ALLWORTH

Is ever open to you. (aside) 'Twas shut till now.aparte

OVERREACH

238Well done, well done, my honorable daughter!
239Thou'rt so already. Know this gentle youth,
240And cherish him, my honorable daughter.

MARGARET

241I shall, with my best care.

Noise within as of a coach.

OVERREACH

I shall, with my best care. A coach!

GREEDY

I shall, with my best care. A coach! More stops
242Before we go to dinner! Oh, my guts!

Enter Lady [Allworth] and Wellborn.

LADY ALLWORTH

Before we go to dinner! Oh, my guts! [privately to Wellborn] If I find welcome,
243You share in it; if not, I'll back again,
244Now I know your ends, for I come armed for all
245Can be objected.

LOVELL

Can be objected. How! The Lady Allworth!

OVERREACH

246And thus attended!

Lovell salutes the Lady [Allworth]; the Lady salutes Margaret.

MARALL

And thus attended! [aside to Overreach] No, I am a dolt!aparte
247The spirit of lies had ent'red me!

OVERREACH

The spirit of lies had ent'red me! [aside to Marall] Peace, patch!aparte
248'Tis more than wonder! An astonishment
249That does possess me wholly!

LOVELL

That does possess me wholly! Noble lady,
250This is a favor, to prevent my visit,
251The service of my life can never equal.

LADY ALLWORTH

252My lord, I laid wait for you, and much hoped
253You would have made my poor house your first inn;
254And therefore doubting that you might forget me,
255Or too long dwell here, having such ample cause
256In this unequalled beauty for your stay,
257And fearing to trust any but myself
258With the relation of my service to you,
259I borrowed so much from my long restraint
260And took the air in person to invite you.

LOVELL

261Your bounties are so great they rob me, madam,
262Of words to give you thanks.

LADY ALLWORTH

Of words to give you thanks. Good Sir Giles Overreach!

Salutes him.

263How dost thou, Marrall? [To Greedy] Liked you my meat so ill
264You'll dine no more with me?

GREEDY

You'll dine no more with me? I will, when you please,
265And it like Your Ladyship.

LADY ALLWORTH

And it like Your Ladyship. When you please, Master Greedy;
266If meat can do it, you shall be satisfied.—
267And now, my lord, pray take into your knowledge
268This gentleman. (Presents Wellborn.) Howe'er his outside's coarse,
269His inward linings are as fine and fair
270As any man's. Wonder not I speak at large.
271And howsoe'er his humor carries him
272To be thus accoutred, or what taint soever
273For his wild life hath stuck upon his fame,
274He may, ere long, with boldness rank himself
275With some that have contemned him.—Sir Giles Overreach,
276If I am welcome, bid him so.

OVERREACH

If I am welcome, bid him so. My nephew!
277He has been too long a stranger. [To Wellborn] Faith, you have;
278Pray, let it be mended.

Lovell conferring [privately] with Wellborn.

MARALL

Pray, let it be mended. [aside to Overreach] Why, sir, what do you mean?aparte
279This is rogue Wellborn, monster, prodigy,
280That should hang or drown himself, no man of worship,
281Much less your nephew.

OVERREACH

Much less your nephew. [aside to Marall] Well, sirrah, we shall reckonaparte
282For this hereafter.

MARALL

For this hereafter. [aside] I'll not lose my jeer,aparte
283Though I be beaten dead for't.

WELLBORN

Though I be beaten dead for't. [privately to Lovell] Let my silence plead
284In my excuse, my lord, till better leisure
285Offer itself to hear a full relation
286Of my poor fortunes.

LOVELL

Of my poor fortunes. [privately to Wellborn] I would hear, and help 'em.

OVERREACH

287[aloud] Your dinner waits you.

LOVELL

[aloud] Your dinner waits you. Pray you lead; we follow.

LADY ALLWORTH
