288[to Wellborn, as he hesitates] Nay, you are my guest. Come, dear Master Wellborn.

Exeunt. Manet Greedy.

GREEDY

289"Dear Master Wellborn"! So she said. Heav'n! Heav'n!
290If my belly would give me leave, I could ruminate
291All day on this. I have granted twenty warrants
292To have him committed, from all prisons in the shire
293To Nottingham jail; and now "Dear Master Wellborn"!
294And "My good nephew"! But I play the fool
295To stand here prating, and forget my dinner.

Enter Marall.

296Are they set, Marrall?

MARALL

Are they set, Marrall? Long since. Pray you a word, sir.

GREEDY

297No wording now.

MARALL

No wording now. In troth, I must. My master,
298Knowing you are his good friend, makes bold with you
299And does entreat you, more guests being come in
300Than he expected, especially his nephew,
301The table being full too, you would excuse him
302And sup with him on the cold meat.

GREEDY

And sup with him on the cold meat. How! No dinner,
303After all my care?

MARALL

After all my care? 'Tis but a penance for
304A meal. Besides, you broke your fast.

GREEDY

A meal. Besides, you broke your fast. That was
305But a bit to stay my stomach. A man in commission
306Give place to a tatterdemalion?

MARALL

Give place to a tatterdemalion? No bug-words, sir.
307Should His Worship hear you—

GREEDY

Should His Worship hear you— Lose my dumpling too?
308And buttered toasts, and woodcocks?

MARALL

And buttered toasts, and woodcocks? Come, have patience.
309If you will dispense a little with your worship,
310And sit with the waiting-women, you have dumpling,
311Woodcock, and buttered toasts too.

GREEDY

Woodcock, and buttered toasts too. This revives me.
312I will gorge there sufficiently.

MARALL

I will gorge there sufficiently. This is the way, sir.

Exeunt.

3.3

[Enter] Overreach as from dinner.

OVERREACH

1She's caught! Oh, women! She neglects my lord,
2And all her compliments applied to Wellborn!
3The garments of her widowhood laid by,
4She now appears as glorious as the spring.
5Her eyes fixed on him, in the wine she drinks,
6He being her pledge, she sends him burning kisses,
7And sits on thorns till she be private with him.
8She leaves my meat to feed upon his looks,
9And, if in our discourse he be but named,
10From her a deep sigh follows. But why grieve I
11At this? It makes for me; if she prove his,
12All that is hers is mine, as I will work him.

Enter Marall.

MARALL

13Sir, the whole board is troubled at your rising.

OVERREACH

14No matter; I'll excuse it. Prithee, Marrall,
15Watch an occasion to invite my nephew
16To speak with me in private.

MARALL

To speak with me in private. Who! The rogue
17The lady scorned to look on?

OVERREACH

The lady scorned to look on? You are a wag.

Enter Lady [Allworth] and Wellborn.

MARALL

18[privately to Overreach] See, sir, she's come, and cannot be without him.

LADY ALLWORTH

19[to Overreach] With your favor, sir, after a plenteous dinner,
20I shall make bold to walk a turn or two
21In your rare garden.

OVERREACH

In your rare garden. There's an arbor too,
22If Your Ladyship please to use it.

LADY ALLWORTH

If Your Ladyship please to use it. Come, Master Wellborn.

Exeunt Lady [Allworth] and Wellborn.

OVERREACH

23Grosser and grosser! Now I believe the poet
24Feigned not, but was historical, when he wrote
25Pasiphaë was enamored of a bull.
26This lady's lust's more monstrous.—

Enter Lovell, Margaret, and the rest [including Allworth, Greedy, and servants].

This lady's lust's more monstrous.— My good lord,
27Excuse my manners.

LOVELL

Excuse my manners. There needs none, Sir Giles—
28I may ere long say "father," when it pleases
29My dearest mistress to give warrant to it.

OVERREACH

30She shall seal to it, my lord, and make me happy.

MARGARET

31My lady is returned.

Enter Wellborn and the Lady [Allworth].

LADY ALLWORTH

My lady is returned. [to servants] Provide my coach;
32I'll instantly away.—My thanks, Sir Giles,

[Exeunt servants.]

33For my entertainment.

OVERREACH

For my entertainment. 'Tis your nobleness
34To think it such.

LADY ALLWORTH

To think it such. I must do you a further wrong
35In taking away your honorable guest.

LOVELL

36I wait on you, madam.—Farewell, good Sir Giles.

LADY ALLWORTH

37Good Mistress Margaret!—Nay, come, Master Wellborn,
38I must not leave you behind; in sooth, I must not.

OVERREACH

39Rob me not, madam, of all joys at once.
40Let my nephew stay behind; he shall have my coach,
41And, after some small conference between us,
42Soon overtake Your Ladyship.

LADY ALLWORTH

Soon overtake Your Ladyship. [to Wellborn] Stay not long, sir.

LOVELL

43[kissing Margaret] This parting kiss. You shall every day hear from me
44By my faithful page.

ALLWORTH

By my faithful page. 'Tis a service I am proud of.

Exeunt Lovell, Lady Allworth, Marall [and all the others except Overreach and Wellborn].

OVERREACH

45Daughter, to your chamber.

[Exit] Margaret.

46You may wonder, nephew,
47After so long an enmity between us,
48I should desire your friendship.

WELLBORN

I should desire your friendship. So I do, sir.
49'Tis strange to me.

OVERREACH

'Tis strange to me. But I'll make it no wonder,
50And, what is more, unfold my nature to you.
51We worldly men, when we see friends and kinsmen
52Past hope sunk in their fortunes, lend no hand
53To lift 'em up, but rather set our feet
54Upon their heads to press 'em to the bottom—
55As, I must yield, with you I practised it.
56But, now I see you in a way to rise,
57I can and will assist you. This rich lady
58(And I am glad of 't) is enamored of you;
59'Tis too apparent, nephew.

WELLBORN

'Tis too apparent, nephew. No such thing;
60Compassion rather, sir.

OVERREACH

Compassion rather, sir. Well, in a word,
61Because your stay is short, I'll have you seen
62No more in this base shape; nor shall she say
63She married you like a beggar, or in debt.

WELLBORN

64(aside) He'll run into the noose and save my labor.aparte

OVERREACH

65You have a trunk of rich clothes, not far hence,
66In pawn; I will redeem 'em. And, that no clamor
67May taint your credit for your petty debts,
68You shall have a thousand pounds to cut 'em off,
69And go a free man to the wealthy lady.

WELLBORN

70This done, sir, out of love, and no ends else—

OVERREACH

71As it is, nephew.

WELLBORN

As it is, nephew. Binds me still your servant.

OVERREACH

72No compliments; you are stayed for. Ere you've supped
73You shall hear from me.—My coach, knaves, for my nephew!—
74Tomorrow I will visit you.

WELLBORN

Tomorrow I will visit you. Here's an uncle
75In a man's extremes! How much they do belie you
76That say you are hard-hearted!

OVERREACH

That say you are hard-hearted! My deeds, nephew,
77Shall speak my love; what men report I weigh not.

Exeunt.

4.1

[Enter] Lovell [and] Allworth.

LOVELL

1'Tis well; give me my cloak. I now discharge you
2From further service. Mind your own affairs;
3I hope they will prove successful.

ALLWORTH

I hope they will prove successful. What is blest
4With your good wish, my lord, cannot but prosper.
5Let aftertimes report, and to your honor,
6How much I stand engaged, for I want language
7To speak my debt. Yet if a tear or two
8Of joy for your much goodness can supply
9My tongue's defects, I could—

LOVELL

My tongue's defects, I could— Nay, do not melt.
10This ceremonial thanks to me's superfluous.

OVERREACH

This ceremonial thanks to me's superfluous. (within) Is my lord stirring?

LOVELL

11'Tis he. Oh, here's your letter.
'Tis he. Oh, here's your letter. [He gives Allworth a letter.] Let him in.

Enter Overreach, Greedy, [and] Marall.

OVERREACH

12A good day to my lord!

LOVELL

A good day to my lord! You are an early riser,
13Sir Giles.

OVERREACH

Sir Giles. And reason: to attend Your Lordship.

LOVELL

14And you too, Master Greedy, up so soon?

GREEDY

15In troth, my lord, after the sun is up
16I cannot sleep, for I have a foolish stomach
17That croaks for breakfast. With Your Lordship's favor,
18I have a serious question to demand
19Of my worthy friend Sir Giles.

LOVELL

Of my worthy friend Sir Giles. Pray you use your pleasure.

GREEDY

20How far, Sir Giles—and pray you, answer me
21Upon your credit—hold you it to be
22From your manor house to this of my Lady Allworth's?

OVERREACH

23Why, some four mile.

GREEDY

Why, some four mile. How! Four mile? Good Sir Giles,
24Upon your reputation, think better,
25For, if you do abate but one half-quarter
26Of five, you do yourself the greatest wrong
27That can be in the world; for four miles riding
28Could not have raised so huge an appetite
29As I feel gnawing on me.

MARALL

As I feel gnawing on me. Whether you ride
30Or go afoot, you are that way still provided,
31An it please Your Worship.

OVERREACH

An it please Your Worship. How now, sirrah? Prating
32Before my lord? No difference? Go to my nephew;
33See all his debts discharged, and help His Worship
34To fit on his rich suit.

MARALL

To fit on his rich suit. [aside] I may fit you too;aparte
35Tossed like a dog still!

Exit Marall.

LOVELL

Tossed like a dog still! I have writ this morning
36A few lines to my mistress, your fair daughter.

OVERREACH

37'Twill fire her, for she's wholly yours already.—
38[Giving a ring] Sweet Master Allworth, take my ring—'twill carry you
39To her presence, I dare warrant you—and there plead
40For my good lord, if you shall find occasion.
41That done, pray ride to Nottingham; get a license,
42Still by this token.—I'll have it dispatched,
43And suddenly, my lord, that I may say
44My "Honorable," nay, "Right Honorable" daughter.

GREEDY

45[to Allworth] Take my advice, young gentleman; get your breakfast.
46'Tis unwholesome to ride fasting. I'll eat with you,
47And eat to purpose.

OVERREACH

And eat to purpose. Some Fury's in that gut!
48Hungry again! Did you not devour this morning
49A shield of brawn and a barrel of Colchester oysters?

GREEDY

50Why that was, sir, only to scour my stomach—
51A kind of a preparative. [To Allworth] Come, gentleman,
52I will not have you feed like the hangman of Flushing,
53Alone, while I am here.

LOVELL

Alone, while I am here. [to Allworth] Haste your return.

ALLWORTH

54I will not fail, my lord.

GREEDY

I will not fail, my lord. Nor I, to line
55My Christmas coffer.

Exeunt Greedy and Allworth.

OVERREACH

My Christmas coffer. To my wish, we are private.
56I come not to make offer with my daughter
57A certain portion; that were poor and trivial.
58In one word, I pronounce all that is mine,
59In lands or leases, ready coin or goods,
60With her, my lord, comes to you; nor shall you have
61One motive to induce you to believe
62I live too long, since every year I'll add
63Something unto the heap which shall be yours too.

LOVELL

64You are a right kind father.

OVERREACH

You are a right kind father. You shall have reason
65To think me such. How do you like this seat?
66It is well wooded and well watered, the acres
67Fertile and rich. Would it not serve for change
68To entertain your friends in a summer progress?
69What thinks my noble lord?

LOVELL

What thinks my noble lord? 'Tis a wholesome air,
70And well-built pile, and she that's mistress of it
71Worthy the large revenue.

OVERREACH

Worthy the large revenue. She the mistress?
72It may be so for a time; but let my lord
73Say only that he likes it and would have it,
74I say, ere long 'tis his.

LOVELL

I say, ere long 'tis his. Impossible.

OVERREACH

75You do conclude too fast, not knowing me,
76Nor the engines that I work by. 'Tis not alone
77The Lady Allworth's lands, for those once Wellborn's
78(As, by her dotage on him, I know they will be)
79Shall soon be mine; but point out any man's
80In all the shire, and say they lie convenient
81And useful for Your Lordship, and once more
82I say aloud, they are yours.

LOVELL

I say aloud, they are yours. I dare not own
83What's by unjust and cruel means extorted;
84My fame and credit are more dear to me
85Than so to expose 'em to be censured by
86The public voice.

OVERREACH

The public voice. You run, my lord, no hazard.
87Your reputation shall stand as fair
88In all good men's opinions as now;
89Nor can my actions, though condemned for ill,
90Cast any foul aspersion upon yours.
91For, though I do contemn report myself
92As a mere sound, I still will be so tender
93Of what concerns you in all points of honor
94That the immaculate whiteness of your fame
95Nor your unquestioned integrity
96Shall e'er be sullied with one taint or spot
97That may take from your innocence and candor.
98All my ambition is to have my daughter
99Right Honorable, which my lord can make her.
100And, might I live to dance upon my knee
101A young Lord Lovell, born by her unto you,
102I write nil ultra to my proudest hopes.
103As for possessions and annual rents
104Equivalent to maintain you in the port
105Your noble birth and present state requires,
106I do remove that burthen from your shoulders
107And take it on mine own; for, though I ruin
108The country to supply your riotous waste,
109The scourge of prodigals—want—shall never find you.

LOVELL

110Are you not frighted with the imprecations
111And curses of whole families made wretched
112By your sinister practices?

OVERREACH

By your sinister practices? Yes, as rocks are
113When foamy billows split themselves against
114Their flinty ribs, or as the moon is moved
115When wolves, with hunger pined, howl at her brightness.
116I am of a solid temper, and, like these,
117Steer on a constant course. With mine own sword,
118If called into the field, I can make that right
119Which fearful enemies murmured at as wrong.
120Now, for these other piddling complaints
121Breathed out in bitterness, as when they call me
122Extortioner, tyrant, cormorant, or intruder
123On my poor neighbor's right, or grand encloser
124Of what was common to my private use;
125Nay, when my ears are pierced with widows' cries,
126And undone orphans wash with tears my threshold:
127I only think what 'tis to have my daughter
128Right Honorable, and 'tis a powerful charm
129Makes me insensible of remorse, or pity,
130Or the least sting of conscience.

LOVELL

Or the least sting of conscience. I admire
131The toughness of your nature.

OVERREACH

The toughness of your nature. 'Tis for you,
132My lord, and for my daughter, I am marble.
133Nay, more: if you will have my character
134In little, I enjoy more true delight
135In my arrival to my wealth these dark
136And crooked ways than you shall e'er take pleasure
137In spending what my industry hath compassed.
138My haste commands me hence. In one word therefore:
139Is it a match?

LOVELL

Is it a match? I hope that is past doubt now.

OVERREACH

140Then rest secure. Not the hate of all mankind here,
141Nor fear of what can fall on me hereafter,
142Shall make me study aught but your advancement
143One story higher. An earl, if gold can do it!
144Dispute not my religion nor my faith.
145Though I am borne thus headlong by my will,
146You may make choice of what belief you please;
147To me they are equal. So, my lord, good morrow.

Exit.

LOVELL

148He's gone. I wonder how the earth can bear
149Such a portent! I, that have lived a soldier,
150And stood the enemy's violent charge undaunted,
151To hear this blasphemous beast am bathed all over
152In a cold sweat. Yet, like a mountain, he,
153Confirmed in atheistical assertions,
154Is no more shaken than Olympus is
155When angry Boreas loads his double head
156With sudden drifts of snow.

Enter Amble, Lady [Allworth, and Waiting-]woman.

LADY ALLWORTH

With sudden drifts of snow. Save you, my lord!
157Disturb I not your privacy?

LOVELL

Disturb I not your privacy? No, good madam.
158For your own sake I am glad you came no sooner,
159Since this bold, bad man, Sir Giles Overreach,
160Made such a plain discovery of himself,
161And read this morning such a devilish matins
162That I should think it a sin next to his
163But to repeat it.

LADY ALLWORTH

But to repeat it. I ne'er pressed, my lord,
164On others' privacies; yet, against my will,
165Walking for health sake in the gallery
166Adjoining to your lodgings, I was made
167(So vehement and loud he was) partaker
168Of his tempting offers.

LOVELL

Of his tempting offers. Please you to command
169Your servants hence, and I shall gladly hear
170Your wiser counsel.

LADY ALLWORTH

Your wiser counsel. 'Tis, my lord, a woman's,
171But true and hearty. [To her servants] Wait in the next room,
172But be within call, yet not so near to force me
173To whisper my intents.

AMBLE

To whisper my intents. We are taught better
174By you, good madam.

WAITING-WOMAN

By you, good madam. And well know our distance.

LADY ALLWORTH

175Do so, and talk not; 'twill become your breeding.

Exeunt Amble and [Waiting-]woman.

176Now, my good lord—if I may use my freedom
177As to an honored friend?

LOVELL

As to an honored friend? You lessen else
178Your favor to me.

LADY ALLWORTH

Your favor to me. I dare then say thus:
179As you are noble, howe'er common men
180Make sordid wealth the object and sole end
181Of their industrious aims, 'twill not agree
182With those of eminent blood, who are engaged
183More to prefer their honors than to increase
184The state left to 'em by their ancestors,
185To study large additions to their fortunes
186And quite neglect their births; though I must grant
187Riches well got to be a useful servant,
188But a bad master.

LOVELL

But a bad master. Madam, 'tis confessed.
189But what infer you from it?

LADY ALLWORTH

But what infer you from it? This, my lord:
190That as all wrongs, though thrust into one scale,
191Slide of themselves off when right fills the other,
192And cannot bide the trial, so all wealth
193(I mean if ill acquired), cemented to honor
194By virtuous ways achieved and bravely purchased,
195Is but as rubbage poured into a river
196(Howe'er intended to make good the bank),
197Rend'ring the water that was pure before
198Polluted and unwholesome. I allow
199The heir of Sir Giles Overreach, Margaret,
200A maid well qualified, and the richest match
201Our north part can make boast of; yet she cannot,
202With all that she brings with her, fill their mouths
203That never will forget who was her father,
204Or that my husband Allworth's lands and Wellborn's
205(How wrung from both needs now no repetition)
206Were real motives that more worked Your Lordship
207To join your families than her form and virtues.
208You may conceive the rest.

LOVELL

You may conceive the rest. I do, sweet madam,
209And long since have considered it. I know,
210The sum of all that makes a just man happy
211Consists in the well choosing of his wife;
212And there, well to discharge it, does require
213Equality of years, of birth, of fortune.
214For beauty, being poor and not cried up
215By birth or wealth, can truly mix with neither;
216And wealth, where there's such difference in years
217And fair descent, must make the yoke uneasy.
218But I come nearer.

LADY ALLWORTH

But I come nearer. Pray you do, my lord.

LOVELL

219Were Overreach' states thrice centupled, his daughter
220Millions of degrees much fairer than she is,
221Howe'er I might urge precedents to excuse me,
222I would not so adulterate my blood
223By marrying Margaret, and so leave my issue
224Made up of several pieces, one part scarlet
225And the other London blue. In my own tomb
226I will inter my name first.

LADY ALLWORTH

I will inter my name first. (aside) I am glad to hear this.aparte
227[Aloud] Why then, my lord, pretend your marriage to her?
228Dissimulation but ties false knots
229On that straight line by which you hitherto
230Have measured all your actions.

LOVELL

Have measured all your actions. I make answer,
231And aptly, with a question. Wherefore have you,
232That since your husband's death have lived a strict
233And chaste nun's life, on the sudden giv'n yourself
234To visits and entertainments? Think you, madam,
235'Tis not grown public conference? Or the favors
236Which you too prodigally have thrown on Wellborn,
237Being too reserved before, incur not censure?

LADY ALLWORTH

238I am innocent here, and on my life I swear
239My ends are good.

LOVELL

My ends are good. On my soul, so are mine
240To Margaret; but leave both to the event.
241And since this friendly privacy does serve
242But as an offered means unto ourselves
243To search each other farther—you having shown
244Your care of me, I my respect to you—
245Deny me not, but still in chaste words, madam,
246An afternoon's discourse.

LADY ALLWORTH

An afternoon's discourse. So I shall hear you.

[Exeunt.]

4.2

[Enter] Tapwell [and] Froth.

TAPWELL

1Undone, undone! This was your counsel, Froth.

FROTH

2Mine! I defy thee. Did not Master Marrall
3(He has marred all, I am sure) strictly command us,
4On pain of Sir Giles Overreach' displeasure,
5To turn the gentleman out of doors?

TAPWELL

To turn the gentleman out of doors? 'Tis true.
6But now he's his uncle's darling, and has got
7Master Justice Greedy (since he filled his belly)
8At his commandment to do anything.
9Woe, woe to us!

FROTH

Woe, woe to us! He may prove merciful.

TAPWELL

10Troth, we do not deserve it at his hands.
11Though he knew all the passages of our house,
12As the receiving of stol'n goods, and bawdry,
13When he was rogue Wellborn no man would believe him,
14And then his information could not hurt us;
15But, now he is "Right Worshipful" again,
16Who dares but doubt his testimony? Methinks
17I see thee, Froth, already in a cart,
18For a close bawd, thine eyes e'en pelted out
19With dirt and rotten eggs, and my hand hissing
20(If I scape the halter) with the letter R
21Printed upon it.

FROTH

Printed upon it. Would that were the worst!
22That were but nine days' wonder, as for credit,
23We have none to lose; but we shall lose the money
24He owes us, and his custom—there's the hell on't.

TAPWELL

25He has summoned all his creditors by the drum,
26And they swarm about him like so many soldiers
27On the payday, and has found out such a new way
28To pay his old debts as 'tis very likely
29He shall be chronicled for it.

FROTH

He shall be chronicled for it. He deserves it,
30More than ten pageants. But are you sure His Worship
31Comes this way to my lady's?

A cry within: "Brave Master Wellborn!"

TAPWELL

Comes this way to my lady's? Yes, I hear him.

FROTH

32Be ready with your petition and present it
33To His good Grace.

Enter Wellborn in a rich habit, [Marall,] Greedy, Order, Furnace, [and] three Creditors. Tapwell, kneeling, delivers his bill of debt.

WELLBORN

To His good Grace. How's this! Petitioned too?
34But note what miracles the payment of
35A little trash and a rich suit of clothes
36Can work upon these rascals! I shall be,
37I think, Prince Wellborn.

MARALL

I think, Prince Wellborn. When Your Worship's married,
38You may be—I know what I hope to see you.

WELLBORN

39Then look thou for advancement.

MARALL

Then look thou for advancement. To be known
40Your Worship's bailiff is the mark I shoot at.

WELLBORN

41And thou shalt hit it.

MARALL

And thou shalt hit it. Pray you, sir, dispatch
42These needy followers, and, for my admittance,
43Provided you'll defend me from Sir Giles,
44Whose service I am weary of, I'll say something
45You shall give thanks for.

WELLBORN

You shall give thanks for. Fear me not Sir Giles.

This interim, Tapwell and Froth flattering and bribing Justice Greedy.

GREEDY

46Who? Tapwell? I remember thy wife brought me,
47Last New Year's tide, a couple of fat turkeys.

TAPWELL

48And shall do every Christmas, let Your Worship
49But stand my friend now.

GREEDY

But stand my friend now. How? With Master Wellborn?
50I can do anything with him, on such terms.—
51[To Wellborn] See you this honest couple? They are good souls
52As ever drew out faucet. Have they not
53A pair of honest faces?

WELLBORN

A pair of honest faces? I o'erheard you,
54And the bribe he promised. You are cozened in 'em,
55For of all the scum that grew rich by my riots,
56This for a most unthankful knave and this
57For a base bawd and whore have worst deserved me,
58And therefore speak not for 'em. By your place
59You are rather to do me justice. Lend me your ear.
60[aside to him] Forget his turkeys, and call in his license,aparte
61And at the next fair I'll give you a yoke of oxen
62Worth all his poultry.

GREEDY

Worth all his poultry. I am changed on the sudden
63In my opinion. [To Tapwell] Come near. Nearer, rascal!
64[To Wellborn] And, now I view him better, did you e'er see
65One look so like an arch-knave? His very countenance,
66Should an understanding judge but look upon him,
67Would hang him, though he were innocent.

TAPWELL  [and] FROTH

Would hang him, though he were innocent. Worshipful sir!

GREEDY

68No, though the great Turk came, instead of turkeys,
69To beg any favor, I am inexorable.
70Thou hast an ill name. Besides thy musty ale,
71That hath destroyed many of the King's liege people,
72Thou never hadst in thy house, to stay mens' stomachs,
73A piece of Suffolk cheese, or gammon of bacon,
74Or any esculent, as the learnèd call it,
75For their emolument, but sheer drink only.
76For which gross fault, I here do damn thy license,
77Forbidding thee ever to tap or draw;
78For instantly I will, in mine own person,
79Command the constable to pull down thy sign,
80And do it before I eat.

FROTH

And do it before I eat. No mercy?

GREEDY

And do it before I eat. No mercy? Vanish!
81If I show any, may my promised oxen gore me!

TAPWELL

82Unthankful knaves are ever so rewarded.

Exeunt Greedy, Tapwell, [and] Froth.

WELLBORN

83[to the First Creditor] Speak; what are you?

FIRST CREDITOR

[to the First Creditor] Speak; what are you? A decayed vintner, sir,
84That might have thrived, but that Your Worship broke me
85With trusting you with muscadine and eggs,
86And five-pound suppers, with your after-drinkings,
87When you lodged upon the Bankside.

WELLBORN

When you lodged upon the Bankside. I remember.

FIRST CREDITOR

88I have not been hasty, nor e'er laid to arrest you;
89And therefore, sir—

WELLBORN

And therefore, sir— Thou art an honest fellow.
90I'll set thee up again. [To Order] See his bill paid.—
91What are you?

SECOND CREDITOR

What are you? A tailor once, but now mere botcher.
92I gave you credit for a suit of clothes,
93Which was all my stock, but, you failing in payment,
94I was removed from the shop board, and confined
95Under a stall.

WELLBORN

Under a stall. [to Order] See him paid.—And botch no more.

SECOND CREDITOR

96I ask no interest, sir.

WELLBORN

I ask no interest, sir. Such tailors need not;
97If their bills are paid in one-and-twenty year,
98They are seldom losers. [To Third Creditor] Oh, I know thy face;
99Thou wert my surgeon. You must tell no tales;
100Those days are done. I will pay you in private.

ORDER

101[to Furnace] A royal gentleman!

FURNACE

[to Furnace] A royal gentleman! [to Order] Royal as an emperor!
102He'll prove a brave master. My good lady knew
103To choose a man.

WELLBORN

To choose a man. [to Order] See all men else discharged;
104And since old debts are cleared by a new way,
105A little bounty will not misbecome me.

[Giving money to Furnace]

106There's something, honest cook, for thy good breakfasts,

[Giving money to Order]

107And this for your respect. Take't; 'tis good gold,
108And I able to spare it.

ORDER

And I able to spare it. You are too munificent.

FURNACE

109[to the others] He was ever so.

WELLBORN

[to the others] He was ever so. Pray you, on before.

THIRD CREDITOR

[to the others] He was ever so. Pray you, on before. Heaven bless you!

MARALL

110At four o'clock the rest know where to meet me.

Exeunt Order, Furnace, [and] Creditors.

WELLBORN

111Now, Master Marrall, what's the weighty secret
112You promised to impart?

MARALL

You promised to impart? Sir, time nor place
113Allow me to relate each circumstance.
114This only in a word: I know Sir Giles
115Will come upon you for security
116For his thousand pounds, which you must not consent to.
117As he grows in heat—as I am sure he will—
118Be you but rough and say he's in your debt
119Ten times the sum, upon sale of your land.
120I had a hand in't (I speak it to my shame)
121When you were defeated of it.

WELLBORN

When you were defeated of it. That's forgiven.

MARALL

122I shall deserve 't, then. Urge him to produce
123The deed in which you passed it over to him—
124Which I know he'll have about him—to deliver
125To the Lord Lovell, with many other writings
126And present moneys. I'll instruct you further,
127As I wait on Your Worship. If I play not my prize
128To your full content and your uncle's much vexation,
129Hang up Jack Marrall.

WELLBORN

Hang up Jack Marrall. I rely upon thee.

Exeunt.

4.3

[Enter] Allworth [and] Margaret.

ALLWORTH

1Whether to yield the first praise to my lord's
2Unequalled temperance or your constant sweetness,
3That I yet live, my weak hands fastened on
4Hope's anchor, spite of all storms of despair,
5I yet rest doubtful.

MARGARET

I yet rest doubtful. Give it to Lord Lovell,
6For what in him was bounty in me's duty.
7I make but payment of a debt to which
8My vows, in that high office registered,
9Are faithful witnesses.

ALLWORTH

Are faithful witnesses. 'Tis true, my dearest.
10Yet, when I call to mind how many fair ones
11Make willful shipwreck of their faiths and oaths
12To God and man to fill the arms of greatness,
13And you rise up no less than a glorious star,
14To the amazement of the world, that hold out
15Against the stern authority of a father
16And spurn at honor when it comes to court you,
17I am so tender of your good that, faintly,
18With your wrong I can wish myself that right
19You yet are pleased to do me.

MARGARET

You yet are pleased to do me. Yet, and ever.
20To me what's title, when content is wanting?
21Or wealth, raked up together with much care
22And to be kept with more, when the heart pines
23In being dispossessed of what it longs for,
24Beyond the Indian mines? Or the smooth brow
25Of a pleased sire, that slaves me to his will,
26And—so his ravenous humor may be feasted
27By my obedience, and he see me great—
28Leaves to my soul nor faculties nor power
29To make her own election?

ALLWORTH

To make her own election? But the dangers
30That follow the repulse—

MARGARET

That follow the repulse— To me they are nothing.
31Let Allworth love, I cannot be unhappy.
32Suppose the worst, that in his rage he kill me;
33A tear or two by you dropped on my hearse
34In sorrow for my fate will call back life
35So far as but to say that I die yours,
36I then shall rest in peace. Or should he prove
37So cruel as one death would not suffice
38His thirst of vengeance, but with ling'ring torments
39In mind and body I must waste to air
40In poverty joined with banishment, so you share
41In my afflictions (which I dare not wish you),
42So high I prize you, I could undergo 'em
43With such a patience as should look down
44With scorn on his worst malice.

ALLWORTH

With scorn on his worst malice. Heaven avert
45Such trials of your true affection to me!
46Nor will it, unto you that are all mercy,
47Show so much rigor. But since we must run
48Such desperate hazards, let us do our best
49To steer between 'em.

MARGARET

To steer between 'em. Your lord's ours, and sure;
50And, though but a young actor, second me
51In doing to the life what he has plotted;
52The end may yet prove happy. Now, my Allworth—

Enter Overreach [behind].

ALLWORTH

53[aside to her as they see Overreach] To your letter! And put on a seeming anger.aparte

MARGARET

54[aloud] I'll pay my lord all debts due to his title,
55And when, with terms not taking from his honor,
56He does solicit me, I shall gladly hear him.
57But in this peremptory, nay, commanding way,
58T'appoint a meeting, and, without my knowledge,
59A priest to tie the knot can ne'er be undone
60Till death unloose it, is a confidence
61In His Lordship will deceive him.

ALLWORTH

In His Lordship will deceive him. I hope better,
62Good lady.

MARGARET

Good lady. Hope, sir, what you please. For me,
63I must take a safe and secure course. I have
64A father, and, without his full consent,
65Though all lords of the land kneeled for my favor,
66I can grant nothing.

OVERREACH

I can grant nothing. [coming forward] I like this obedience.
67But whatsoever my lord writes must and shall be
68Accepted and embraced. Sweet Master Allworth,
69You show yourself a true and faithful servant
70To your good lord; he has a jewel of you.—
71How? Frowning, Meg? Are these looks to receive
72A messenger from my lord?
73[Seeing the letter] What's this? Give me it.

MARGARET

74A piece of arrogant paper, like th'inscriptions.

Overreach [takes and] read[s] the letter.

OVERREACH

75"Fair mistress, from your servant learn all joys
76That we can hope for, if deferred, prove toys;
77Therefore this instant, and in private, meet
78A husband that will gladly at your feet
79Lay down his honors, tend'ring them to you
80With all content, the church being paid her due."
81Is this the arrogant piece of paper? Fool,
82Will you still be one? In the name of madness, what
83Could His good Honor write more to content you?
84Is there aught else to be wished after these two
85That are already offered: marriage first,
86And lawful pleasure after? What would you more?

MARGARET

87Why, sir, I would be married like your daughter,
88Not hurried away I'th'night I know not whither,
89Without all ceremony, no friends invited
90To honor the solemnity.

ALLWORTH

To honor the solemnity. An't please Your Honor—
91[Aside] For so before tomorrow I must style you—aparte
92My lord desires this privacy in respect
93His honorable kinsmen are far off,
94And his desires to have it done brook not
95So long delay as to expect their coming;
96And yet he stands resolved, with all due pomp—
97As running at the ring, plays, masques, and tilting—
98To have his marriage at court celebrated
99When he has brought Your Honor up to London.

OVERREACH

100[to Margaret] He tells you true; 'tis the fashion, on my knowledge.
101Yet the good lord, to please your peevishness,
102Must put it off, forsooth, and lose a night
103In which perhaps he might get two boys on thee.
104Tempt me no farther. If you do, this goad

[Pointing to his sword]

105Shall prick you to him.

MARGARET

Shall prick you to him. I could be contented,
106Were you but by to do a father's part
107And give me in the church.

OVERREACH

And give me in the church. So my lord have you,
108What do I care who gives you? Since my lord
109Does purpose to be private, I'll not cross him.—
110I know not, Master Allworth, how my lord
111May be provided, and therefore
112[giving money] there's a purse
113Of gold 'twill serve this night's expense; tomorrow
114I'll furnish him with any sums. In the meantime,
115Use my ring to my chaplain; he is beneficed
116At my manor of Gotham, and called Parson Willdo.
117'Tis no matter for a license; I'll bear him out in't.

MARGARET

118With your favor, sir, what warrant is your ring?
119He may suppose I got that twenty ways,
120Without your knowledge; and then to be refused
121Were such a stain upon me! If you pleased, sir,
122Your presence would do better.

OVERREACH

Your presence would do better. Still perverse?
123I say again I will not cross my lord;
124Yet I'll prevent you too.
125[Calling] Paper and ink there!

ALLWORTH

126I can furnish you.

OVERREACH

I can furnish you. I thank you; I can write then.

Writes on his book.

ALLWORTH

127You man, if you please, put out the name of my lord,
128In respect he comes disguised, and only write:
129"Marry her to this gentleman."

OVERREACH

"Marry her to this gentleman." Well advised.

[He writes, and gives the note to Allworth.]

130'Tis done. Away! (Margaret kneels.) My blessing, girl? Thou hast it.
131Nay, no reply; begone. [She rises.] Good Master Allworth,
132This shall be the best night's work you ever made.

ALLWORTH

133I hope so, sir.

Exeunt Allworth and Margaret.

OVERREACH

I hope so, sir. Farewell!—Now all's cocksure.
134Methinks I hear already knights and ladies
135Say, "Sir Giles Overreach, how is it with
136Your honorable daughter? Has Her Honor
137Slept well tonight?" Or, "Will Her Honor please
138To accept this monkey? Dog? Or parakeet?"
139(This is state in ladies), or "My eldest son
140To be her page, and wait upon her trencher?"
141My ends, my ends are compassed! Then for Wellborn
142And the lands. Were he once married to the widow,
143I have him here. I can scarce contain myself,
144I am so full of joy, nay, joy all over!

Exit.

5.1

[Enter] Lovell, Lady [Allworth, and] Amble [who retires once he has ushered them in].

LADY ALLWORTH

1By this you know how strong the motives were
2That did, my lord, induce me to dispense
3A little with my gravity, to advance,
4In personating some few favors to him,
5The plots and projects of the downtrod Wellborn.
6Nor shall I e'er repent—although I suffer
7In some few men's opinions for't—the action.
8For he that ventured all for my dear husband
9Might justly claim an obligation from me
10To pay him such a courtesy, which, had I
11Coyly or overcuriously denied,
12It might have argued me of little love
13To the deceased.

LOVELL

To the deceased. What you intended, madam,
14For the poor gentleman hath found good success,
15For, as I understand, his debts are paid,
16And he once more furnished for fair employment.
17But all the arts that I have used to raise
18The fortunes of your joy and mine, young Allworth,
19Stand yet in supposition, though I hope well,
20For the young lovers are in wit more pregnant
21Than their years can promise; and for their desires,
22On my knowledge, they are equal.

LADY ALLWORTH

On my knowledge, they are equal. As my wishes
23Are with yours, my lord. Yet give me leave to fear
24The building, though well grounded. To deceive
25Sir Giles, that's both a lion and a fox
26In his proceedings, were a work beyond
27The strongest undertakers, not the trial
28Of two weak innocents.

LOVELL

Of two weak innocents. Despair not, madam.
29Hard things are compassed oft by easy means,
30And judgment, being a gift derived from heaven,
31Though sometimes lodged I'th'hearts of worldly men
32That ne'er consider from whom they receive it,
33Forsakes such as abuse the giver of it.
34Which is the reason that the politic
35And cunning statesman, that believes he fathoms
36The counsels of all kingdoms on the earth,
37Is by simplicity oft overreached.

LADY ALLWORTH

38May he be so! Yet in his name to express it
39Is a good omen.

LOVELL

Is a good omen. May it to myself
40Prove so, good lady, in my suit to you!
41What think you of the motion?

LADY ALLWORTH

What think you of the motion? Troth, my lord,
42My own unworthiness may answer for me;
43For had you, when that I was in my prime
44(My virgin flower uncropped), presented me
45With this great favor, looking on my lowness
46Not in a glass of self-love but of truth,
47I could not but have thought it as a blessing
48Far, far beyond my merit.

LOVELL

Far, far beyond my merit. You are too modest,
49And undervalue that which is above
50My title, or whatever I call mine.
51I grant, were I a Spaniard, to marry
52A widow might disparage me, but, being
53A trueborn Englishman, I cannot find
54How it can taint my honor. Nay, what's more,
55That which you think a blemish is to me
56The fairest lustre. You already, madam,
57Have given sure proofs how dearly you can cherish
58A husband that deserves you, which confirms me
59That, if I am not wanting in my care
60To do you service, you'll be still the same
61That you were to your Allworth. In a word,
62Our years, our states, our births are not unequal,
63You being descended nobly and allied so.
64If then you may be won to make me happy,
65But join your lips to mine, and that shall be
66A solemn contract.

LADY ALLWORTH

A solemn contract. I were blind to my own good,
67Should I refuse it.
68[They kiss.] Yet, my lord, receive me
69As such a one the study of whose whole life
70Shall know no other object but to please you.

LOVELL

71If I return not, with all tenderness,
72Equal respect to you, may I die wretched!

LADY ALLWORTH

73There needs no protestation, my lord.
74To her that cannot doubt—

Enter Wellborn [handsomely dressed].

To her that cannot doubt— You are welcome, sir.
75Now you look like yourself.

WELLBORN

Now you look like yourself. And will continue
76Such, in my free acknowledgment that I am
77Your creature, madam, and will never hold
78My life mine own when you please to command it.

LOVELL

79It is a thankfulness that well becomes you.
80You could not make choice of a better shape
81To dress your mind in.

LADY ALLWORTH

To dress your mind in. For me, I am happy
82That my endeavors prospered. Saw you of late
83Sir Giles, your uncle?

WELLBORN

Sir Giles, your uncle? I heard of him, madam,
84By his minister, Marrall. He's grown into strange passions
85About his daughter. This last night he looked for
86Your Lordship at his house, but, missing you,
87And she not yet appearing, His Wisehead
88Is much perplexed and troubled.

LOVELL

Is much perplexed and troubled. [to Lady Allworth] It may be,
89Sweetheart, my project took.

Enter Overreach [with a box], with distracted looks, driving in Marall before him. [They are unaware at first of the presence of the others already onstage.]

LADY ALLWORTH

Sweetheart, my project took. I strongly hope.

OVERREACH

90[to Marall] Ha! find her, booby, thou huge lump of nothing!
91I'll bore thine eyes out else.

WELLBORN

I'll bore thine eyes out else. [aside to Lovell] May it please Your Lordship,aparte
92For some ends of mine own, but to withdraw
93A little out of sight, though not of hearing,
94You may perhaps have sport.

LOVELL

You may perhaps have sport. You shall direct me.

Steps aside.

OVERREACH

95[to Marall] I shall sol-fa you, rogue.

MARALL

[to Marall] I shall sol-fa you, rogue. Sir, for what cause
96Do you use me thus?

OVERREACH

Do you use me thus? Cause, slave? Why, I am angry,
97And thou a subject only fit for beating,
98And so to cool my choler. Look to the writing;
99Let but the seal be broke upon the box
100That has slept in my cabinet these three years,
101I'll rack thy soul for't.

MARALL

I'll rack thy soul for't. (aside) I may yet cry quittance,aparte
102Though now I suffer and dare not resist.

OVERREACH

Though now I suffer and dare not resist. [seeing Lady Allworth] Lady, by your leave, did you see my daughter, lady?
103And the lord her husband? Are they in your house?
104If they are, discover, that I may bid 'em joy;
105And, as an entrance to her place of honor,
106See Your Ladyship on her left hand, and make curtsies
107When she nods on you, which you must receive
108As a special favor.

LADY ALLWORTH

As a special favor. When I know, Sir Giles,
109Her state requires such ceremony, I shall pay it;
110But in the meantime, as I am myself,
111I give you to understand I neither know
112Nor care where Her Honor is.

OVERREACH

Nor care where Her Honor is. When you once see her
113Supported and led by the lord her husband,
114You'll be taught better.
You'll be taught better. [Seeing Wellborn] Nephew!

WELLBORN

You'll be taught better. [Seeing Wellborn] Nephew! Sir.

OVERREACH

You'll be taught better. [Seeing Wellborn] Nephew! Sir. No more?

WELLBORN

115'Tis all I owe you.

OVERREACH

'Tis all I owe you. Have you redeemed rags
116Made you thus insolent?

WELLBORN

Made you thus insolent? (in scorn) Insolent to you?
117Why, what are you, sir, unless in your years,
118At the best, more than myself?

OVERREACH

At the best, more than myself? [aside] His fortune swells him.aparte
119'Tis rank he's married.

LADY ALLWORTH

'Tis rank he's married. This is excellent!

OVERREACH

120Sir, in calm language (though I seldom use it),
121I am familiar with the cause that makes you
122Bear up thus bravely. There's a certain buzz
123Of a stol'n marriage—do you hear?—of a stol'n marriage,
124In which, 'tis said, there's somebody hath been cozened.
125I name no parties.

WELLBORN

I name no parties. Well, sir, and what follows?

OVERREACH

126Marry, this, since you are peremptory: remember,
127Upon mere hope of your great match, I lent you
128A thousand pounds. Put me in good security,
129And suddenly, by mortgage or by statute
130Of some of your new possessions, or I'll have you
131Dragged in your lavender robes to the jail. You know me,
132And therefore do not trifle.

WELLBORN

And therefore do not trifle. Can you be
133So cruel to your nephew, now he's in
134The way to rise? Was this the courtesy
135You did me in pure love and no ends else?

OVERREACH

136End me no ends! Engage the whole estate,
137And force you spouse to sign it, you shall have
138Three or four thousand more, to roar and swagger
139And revel in bawdy taverns.

WELLBORN

And revel in bawdy taverns. And beg after;
140Mean you not so?

OVERREACH

Mean you not so? My thoughts are mine, and free.
141Shall I have security?

WELLBORN

Shall I have security? No, indeed you shall not,
142Nor bond, nor bill, nor bare acknowledgment.
143Your great looks fright not me.

OVERREACH

Your great looks fright not me. But my deeds shall.
144Outbraved?

They both draw.

The servants [including Order, Amble, and Furnace] enter.

LADY ALLWORTH

Outbraved? Help! Murder, murder!

WELLBORN

Outbraved? Help! Murder, murder! Let him come on,
145With all his wrongs and injuries about him,
146Armed with his cutthroat practices to guard him;
147The right that I bring with me will defend me,
148And punish his extortion.

OVERREACH

And punish his extortion. That I had thee
149But single in the field!

LADY ALLWORTH

But single in the field! You may; but make not
150My house your quarrelling scene.

OVERREACH

My house your quarrelling scene. Were't in a church,
151By heaven, and hell, I'll do't.

MARALL

By heaven, and hell, I'll do't. [aside to Wellborn] Now put him toaparte
152The showing of the deed.

WELLBORN

The showing of the deed. This rage is vain, sir.
153For fighting, fear not; you shall have your hands full
154Upon the least incitement. And whereas
155You charge me with a debt of a thousand pounds,
156If there be law (howe'er you have no conscience),
157Either restore my land, or I'll recover
158A debt that's truly due to me from you
159In value ten times more than what you challenge.

OVERREACH

160I in thy debt? Oh, impudence! Did I not purchase
161The land left by thy father, that rich land,
162That had continued in Wellborn's name
163Twenty descents, which, like a riotous fool,
164Thou didst make sale of? Is not here enclosed
165The deed that does confirm it mine?

MARALL

The deed that does confirm it mine? [aside to Wellborn] Now, now!aparte

WELLBORN

166I do acknowledge none. I ne'er passed o'er
167Any such land. I grant for a year or two
168You had it in trust, which if you do discharge,
169Surrend'ring the possession, you shall ease
170Yourself and me of chargeable suits in law—
171Which if you prove not honest (as I doubt it)
172Must of necessity follow.

LADY ALLWORTH

Must of necessity follow. In my judgment
173He does advise you well.

OVERREACH

He does advise you well. Good! Good! Conspire
174With you new husband, lady; second him
175In his dishonest practices. But when
176This manor is extended to my use,
177You'll speak in an humbler key and sue for favor.

LADY ALLWORTH

178Never. Do not hope it.

WELLBORN

Never. Do not hope it. Let despair first seize me!

OVERREACH

179Yet to shut up thy mouth and make thee give
180Thyself the lie, the loud lie, I draw out
181The precious evidence; if thou canst forswear
182Thy hand and seal, and make a forfeit of
183Thy ears to the pillory, see, here's that will make
184My interest clear.
My interest clear. (Opens the box.) Ha!

LADY ALLWORTH

My interest clear. (Opens the box.) Ha! A fair skin of parchment.

WELLBORN

185Indented, I confess, and labels too,
186But neither wax nor words. How! Thunderstruck?
187Not a syllable to insult with? My wise uncle,
188Is this your precious evidence? Is this that makes
189Your interest clear?

OVERREACH

Your interest clear? I am o'erwhelmed with wonder!
190What prodigy is this? What subtle devil
191Hath razed out the inscription, the wax
192Turned into dust? The rest of my deeds whole
193As when they were delivered, and this only
194Made nothing! Do you deal with witches, rascal?
195There is a statute for you, which will bring
196Your neck in a hempen circle; yes, there is.
197And now 'tis better thought, for, cheater, know
198This juggling shall not save you.

WELLBORN

This juggling shall not save you. To save thee
199Would beggar the stock of mercy.

OVERREACH

Would beggar the stock of mercy. Marrall!

MARALL

Would beggar the stock of mercy. Marrall! Sir?

OVERREACH

200(flattering him) Though the witnesses are dead, your testimony—
201Help with an oath or two; and for thy master,
202Thy liberal master, my good, honest servant,
203I know thou wilt swear anything to dash
204This cunning sleight. Besides, I know thou art
205A public notary, and such stand in law
206For a dozen witnesses. The deed being drawn too
207By thee, my careful Marrall, and delivered
208When thou wert present, will make good my title.
209Wilt thou not swear this?

MARALL

Wilt thou not swear this? I? No, I assure you.
210I have a conscience not seared up like yours;
211I know no deeds.

OVERREACH

I know no deeds. Wilt thou betray me?

MARALL

I know no deeds. Wilt thou betray me? [to the others] Keep him
212From using of his hands, I'll use my tongue
213To his no little torment.

OVERREACH

To his no little torment. [as they restrain him] Mine own varlet
214Rebel against me?

MARALL

Rebel against me? Yes, and uncase you, too.
215The idiot, the patch, the slave, the booby,
216The property fit only to be beaten
217For your morning exercise, your football, or
218Th'unprofitable lump of flesh, your drudge,
219Can now anatomize you, and lay open
220All your black plots, and level with the earth
221Your hill of pride, and, with these gabions guarded,
222Unload my great artillery and shake,
223Nay, pulverize the walls you think defend you.

LADY ALLWORTH

224How he foams at the mouth with rage!

WELLBORN

How he foams at the mouth with rage! To him again.

OVERREACH

225Oh, that I had thee in my grip! I would tear thee
226Joint after joint!

MARALL

Joint after joint! I know you are a tearer,
227But I'll have first your fangs pared off, and then
228Come nearer to you, when I have discovered
229And made it good before the judge what ways
230And devilish practices you used to cozen with
231An army of whole families, who, yet alive
232And but enrolled for soldiers, were able
233To take in Dunkirk.

WELLBORN

To take in Dunkirk. All will come out.

LADY ALLWORTH

To take in Dunkirk. All will come out. The better.

OVERREACH

234But that I will live, rogue, to torture thee
235And make thee wish—and kneel in vain—to die,
236These swords that keep thee from me should fix here,
237Although they made my body but one wound,
238But I would reach thee.

LOVELL

But I would reach thee. (aside) Heav'n's hand is in this!aparte
239One bandog worry the other!

OVERREACH

One bandog worry the other! I play the fool,
240And make my anger but ridiculous.
241There will be a time and place—there will be, cowards!—
242When you shall feel what I dare do.

WELLBORN

When you shall feel what I dare do. I think so.
243You dare do any ill, yet want true valor
244To be honest and repent.

OVERREACH

To be honest and repent. They are words I know not,
245Nor e'er will learn. Patience, the beggar's virtue,
246Shall find no harbor here.

Enter Greedy and Parson Willdo.

Shall find no harbor here. After these storms,
247At length a calm appears. Welcome, most welcome!
248There's comfort in thy looks. Is the deed done?
249Is my daughter married? Say but so, my chaplain,
250And I am tame.

WILLDO

And I am tame. Married? Yes, I assure you.

OVERREACH

251Then vanish all sad thoughts!
Then vanish all sad thoughts! [Offering money] There's more gold for thee.
252My doubts and fears are in the titles drowned
253Of my Right Honorable, my Right Honorable daughter.

GREEDY

254Here will be feasting! At least for a month
255I am provided. Empty guts, croak no more!
256You shall be stuffed like bagpipes, not with wind
257But bearing dishes.

OVERREACH

But bearing dishes. (whispering to Willdo) Instantly be here?
258To my wish, to my wish! Now you that plot against me,
259And hoped to trip my heels up, that contemned me,
260Think on't, and tremble. (Loud music.) They come! I hear the music.
261A lane there for my lord!

WELLBORN

A lane there for my lord! This sudden heat
262May yet be cooled, sir.

OVERREACH

May yet be cooled, sir. Make way there for my lord!

Enter Allworth and Margaret.

MARGARET

263(kneeling) Sir, first your pardon, then your blessing, with
264Your full allowance of the choice I have made,
265As ever you could make use of your reason.
266Grow not in passion, since you may as well
267Call back the day that's past as untie the knot
268Which is too strongly fastened. Not to dwell
269Too long on words, this's my husband.

OVERREACH

Too long on words, this's my husband. How!

ALLWORTH

270So I assure you. All the rites of marriage,
271With every circumstance, are past. Alas, sir,
272Although I am no lord, but a lord's page,
273Your daughter and my loved wife mourns not for it;
274And, for "Right Honorable son-in-law," you may say
275"Your dutiful daughter."

OVERREACH

"Your dutiful daughter." Devil! Are they married?

WILLDO

276Do a father's part, and say, "Heav'n give 'em joy!"

OVERREACH

277Confusion and ruin! Speak, and speak quickly,
278Or thou art dead.

WILLDO

Or thou art dead. They are married.

OVERREACH

Or thou art dead. They are married. Thou hadst better
279Have made a contract with the king of fiends
280Than these. My brain turns!

WILLDO

Than these. My brain turns! Why this rage to me?
281Is not this your letter, sir, and these the words?
282"Marry her to this gentleman."

OVERREACH

"Marry her to this gentleman." It cannot—
283Nor will I e'er believe it—'sdeath, I will not—
284That I, that in all passages I touched
285At worldly profit have not left a print
286Where I have trod for the most curious search
287To trace my footsteps, should be gulled by children,
288Baffled and fooled, and all my hopes and labors
289Defeated and made void!

WELLBORN

Defeated and made void! As it appears,
290You are so, my grave uncle.

OVERREACH

You are so, my grave uncle. Village nurses
291Revenge their wrongs with curses. I'll not waste
292A syllable, but thus I take the life
293Which wretched I gave to thee.

Offers to kill Margaret.

LOVELL

Which wretched I gave to thee. [intervening] Hold, for your own sake!
294Though charity to your daughter hath quite left you,
295Will you do an act, though in your hopes lost here,
296Can leave no hope for peace or rest hereafter?
297Consider: at the best you are but a man,
298And cannot so create your aims but that
299They may be crossed.

OVERREACH

They may be crossed. Lord, thus I spit at thee
300And at thy counsel, and again desire thee,
301As thou art a soldier, if thy valor
302Dares show itself where multitude and example
303Lead not the way, let's quit the house and change
304Six words in private.

LOVELL

Six words in private. I am ready, sir.

LADY ALLWORTH

Six words in private. I am ready, sir. [to Lovell] Stay, sir!
305Contest with one distracted?

WELLBORN

Contest with one distracted? You'll grow like him,
306Should you answer his vain challenge.

OVERREACH

Should you answer his vain challenge. [to Lovell] Are you pale?
307Borrow his help. Though Hercules call it odds,
308I'll stand against both, as I am, hemmed in thus.
309Since, like a Libyan lion in the toil,
310My fury cannot reach the coward hunters
311And only spends itself, I'll quit the place.
312Alone I can do nothing, but I have servants
313And friends to second me; and, if I make not
314This house a heap of ashes—by my wrongs,
315What I have spoke I will make good!—or leave
316One throat uncut, if it be possible,
317Hell add to my afflictions!

Exit Overreach.

MARALL

Hell add to my afflictions! Is't not brave sport?

GREEDY

318Brave sport? I am sure it has ta'en away my stomach;
319I do not like the sauce.

ALLWORTH

I do not like the sauce. [to Margaret] Nay, weep not, dearest,
320Though it express your pity; what's decreed
321Above, we cannot alter.

LADY ALLWORTH

Above, we cannot alter. His threats move me
322No scruple, madam.

MARALL

No scruple, madam. [to Wellborn] Was it not a rare trick,
323An it please Your Worship, to make the deed nothing?
324I can do twenty neater, if you please
325To purchase and grow rich, for I will be
326Such a solicitor and steward for you
327As never worshipful had.

WELLBORN

As never worshipful had. I do believe thee.
328But first discover the quaint means you used
329To raze out the conveyance.

MARALL

To raze out the conveyance. They are mysteries
330Not to be spoke in public: certain minerals
331Incorporated in the ink and wax.
332Besides, he gave me nothing, but still fed me
333With hopes and blows; and that was the inducement
334To this conundrum. If it please Your Worship
335To call to memory, this mad beast once caused me
336To urge you or to drown or hang yourself;
337I'll do the like to him, if you command me.

WELLBORN

338You are a rascal! He that dares be false
339To a master, though unjust, will ne'er be true
340To any other. Look not for reward
341Or favor from me; I will shun thy sight
342As I would do a basilisk's. Thank my pity
343If thou keep thy ears. Howe'er, I will take order
344Your practice shall be silenced.

GREEDY

Your practice shall be silenced. I'll commit him,
345If you'll have me, sir.

WELLBORN

346That were to little purpose.
347His conscience be his prison.—Not a word,
348But instantly begone!

ORDER

But instantly begone! [kicking Marall] Take this kick with you.

AMBLE

349[kicking Marall] And this.

FURNACE

[kicking Marall] And this. If that I had my cleaver here
350I would divide your knave's head.

MARALL

I would divide your knave's head. This is the haven
351False servants still arrive at.

Exit Marall.

Enter Overreach [distracted in his wits].

LADY ALLWORTH

False servants still arrive at. Come again!

LOVELL

352Fear not; I am your guard.

WELLBORN

Fear not; I am your guard. His looks are ghastly.

WILLDO

353Some little time I have spent, under your favors,
354In physical studies, and, if my judgment err not,
355He's mad beyond recovery. But observe him,
356And look to yourselves.

OVERREACH

And look to yourselves. Why, is not the whole world
357Included in myself? To what use then
358Are friends and servants? Say there were a squadron
359Of pikes, lined through with shot; when I am mounted
360Upon my injuries, shall I fear to charge 'em?

Flourishing his sword ensheathed.

361No: I'll through the battalia, and, that routed,
362I'll fall to execution. Ha! I am feeble:
363Some undone widow sits upon mine arm
364And takes away the use of't, and my sword,
365Glued to my scabbard with wronged orphans' tears,
366Will not be drawn. Ha! What are these? Sure, hangmen,
367That come to bind my hands, and then to drag me
368Before the judgment seat! Now they are new shapes
369And do appear like Furies, with steel whips
370To scourge my ulcerous soul! Shall I then fall
371Ingloriously, and yield? No! Spite of Fate,
372I will be forced to hell like to myself;
373Though you were legions of accursèd spirits,
374Thus would I fly among you.

[He runs at them weakly.]

WELLBORN

Thus would I fly among you. There's no help.
375Disarm him first, then bind him.

GREEDY

Disarm him first, then bind him. Take a mittimus
376And carry him to Bedlam.

LOVELL

And carry him to Bedlam. How he foams!

WELLBORN

377And bites the earth!

WILLDO

378Carry him to some dark room.
379There try what art can do for his recovery.

MARGARET

380O my dear father!

They [Order, Amble, Furnace, etc.] force Overreach off.

ALLWORTH

O my dear father! You must be patient, mistress.

LOVELL

381Here is a precedent to teach wicked men
382That, when they leave religion and turn atheists,
383Their own abilities leave 'em. Pray you, take comfort.
384I will endeavor you shall be his guardians
385In his distractions. And for your land, Master Wellborn,
386Be it good or ill in law, I'll be an umpire
387Between you and this, th'undoubted heir
388Of Sir Giles Overreach. For me, here's the anchor
389That I must fix on.

ALLWORTH

That I must fix on. What you shall determine,
390My lord, I will allow of.

WELLBORN

My lord, I will allow of. 'Tis the language
391That I speak, too. But there is something else
392Beside the repossession of my land
393And payment of my debts that I must practice.
394I had a reputation, but 'twas lost
395In my loose course; and, till I redeem it
396Some noble way, I am but half made up.
397It is a time of action. If Your Lordship
398Will please to confer a company upon me
399In your command, I doubt not in my service
400To my king and country but I shall do something
401That may make me right again.

LOVELL

That may make me right again. Your suit is granted,
402And you loved for the motion.

WELLBORN

And you loved for the motion. Nothing wants then
403But your allowance—

The Epilogue

1But your allowance, and in that our all
2Is comprehended, it being known nor we
3Nor he that wrote the comedy can be free
4Without your manumission—which if you
5Grant willingly, as a fair favor due
6To the poet's and our labors (as you may,
7For we despair not, gentlemen, of the play),
8We jointly shall profess Your Grace hath might
9To teach us action, and him how to write.

[Exeunt.]

Escena I

[Ante la casa de BONASPITA]

[Entran] BENNATO [con ropas harapientas,] BONASPITA y ESPUMA.

y os llevaríais vos el nombre. ¡¿Cómo, perro?! Mismamente, señor.

vuestro harapiento, piojoso— ¡Truhán! ¡Esclavo! Sin ira, señor.

no lleva otro registro. ¿No soy yo aquel

siervo en su casa? Lo que fui, señor, no hace al caso;

40Señorito Francisco de antaño, desamparado Bennato ahora—

41¡Alto, esclavo, o me perderé!

¡Alto, esclavo, o me perderé! Difícilmente

podríais estar más perdido. Pero, volviendo a mi relato:

y vos la habéis estudiado. Todavía no he terminado.

en vuestros días. A fustazos te secaré el seso.

paloteadores nocturnos. Cierto, pero aportaron beneficio

y le daréis las gracias a aquí mi Señoría. Así, virote

y así — [a ESPUMA] ¡Pide auxilio!

y así — [a ESPUMA] ¡Pide auxilio! Muévete y mueres.

en oro contante. ¡Niégalo, desgraciado! He de hacerlo, señor;

si se volvieron pobres como vos. Tienen su buena recompensa

sin dejar un hueso entero. ¡Ah!

91No será concedida.
